sources.news_title: Dr. Anthony Fauci declines to testify at COVID-19 hearing, invokes U.S. Constitution
sources.text: WASHINGTON -- Dr. Anthony Fauci on Wednesday repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer dozens of questions from senators in a Republican-led committee hearing about his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. The decision, at least for now, shielded Fauci from answering questions that could expose him to accusations of lying under oath. Though he received a pardon in early 2025 from Democratic U.S. president Joe Biden, some Republicans pursuing a yearslong campaign for his arrest had suggested he could still face charges for any perjury committed during Wednesday’s hearing. The scientist, who helped lead the nation’s COVID-19 response, was subpoenaed to testify under oath by Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had an antagonistic relationship with Fauci. In response to angry, sometimes mocking, questions from Republican senators, Fauci declined to answer more than 100 times, injecting new drama into partisan divides that have festered for years about the origins and handling of the pandemic. Fauci himself has become a polarizing figure, even receiving death threats that prompted him to seek security. In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution.” “The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, behind bars, unquote.” Fauci said, adding that while it pained him to do so, he was following his attorney’s advice by taking the Fifth. Paul, who has long argued that Fauci should be criminally investigated, based on his belief that the scientist was dishonest in previous testimony to Congress, announced that the committee will vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt for declining to answer questions. He did not say whether he would push for a criminal contempt referral to federal prosecutors or another charge. He also raised questions about whether Fauci’s pardon affects his eligibility for Fifth Amendment protections. Republicans accuse Fauci of lying while Democrats say he didn’t deserve that In the combative hearing, Paul and other Republicans accused Fauci of lying in earlier testimony about the origins of the coronavirus, something the longtime National Institutes of Health scientist has forcefully denied. Democrats called the hearing a politically motivated attempt at entrapping Fauci and praised the scientist for his work during the pandemic. With Fauci declining to answer questions throughout, Paul dominated the approximately three-hour hearing, listing a litany of accusations and detailed questions. “Today will be the capstone to Anthony Fauci’s 40 years of abuse of power at NIH,” Paul said. “History will judge, but the facts as we now know them paint a sordid tale of dishonesty, misjudgment and ultimately the hubris, the likes of which the world has never seen.” In a heated moment during the hearing, Paul ejected Fauci’s attorney, David Schertler, from the room after he tried to speak without being recognized. In a statement, Schertler said the removal was “outrageous and demonstrates the completely biased and baseless nature of this proceeding.” In another statement, he called Paul’s accusations about Fauci “false and disgraceful.” Democratic senators praised Fauci and said he didn’t deserve the treatment he was getting. “This hearing is designed to entrap you,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire. Paul releases some of Fauci’s diary Leading up to the hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary covering the pandemic years. Pointing to some notes about early efforts at understanding how the virus emerged, Paul said on social media that what Fauci “wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories.” Some of the diary entries -- including Fauci’s uncertainty in the pandemic’s earliest days as scientists around the world raced to understand the new virus and how best to curb it before vaccines could be created -- already were reflected in a 2024 memoir and in interviews at the time. But they have nonetheless drawn attention from people who blame Fauci for mask mandates, school closures and other policies they believe infringed on their rights as hundreds of thousands of people were dying. U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday wrote on social media that he stopped relying on Fauci over the course of the pandemic because he felt the scientist made bad decisions about masks, shutdowns, and other issues. He later told reporters he watched the entire hearing. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist before entering public office, said on social media that his department had found the diary entries on government property and had given them to the committee. Dozens of disease experts defend Fauci Scientists also scrambled to Fauci’s defence ahead of the unusual hearing -- the second time he has been back before Congress to discuss pandemic origins since leaving the government in 2022. While the COVID-19 pandemic introduced him to millions of Americans, he talked the nation through numerous outbreaks over decades, including HIV, Ebola and the 2001 anthrax attacks, while advising seven presidents. In a public letter, more than 150 infectious-disease experts and other scientists wrote that “no credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges” and that they are “urging our elected representatives in Congress stop these witch-hunts.” Among topics discussed at Wednesday’s hearing was whether NIH-funded research in China may have played a role in how the pandemic started. Many scientists believe the virus most likely emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people, coming to light when it spread at a wildlife market in the Chinese city of Wuhan. There’s no new scientific information supporting that the virus might instead have leaked from a laboratory, a theory Paul champions. A GOP-led subcommittee that studied the question in 2024 did not find any evidence linking Fauci to wrongdoing. Fauci has long said publicly that he was open to both theories but that there’s more evidence supporting COVID-19’s natural origins. Republicans also have accused Fauci of lying about whether his agency funded what’s known as gain of function research -- the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impact -- at a lab in Wuhan. The NIH for years gave grants to a New York nonprofit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to work with a Chinese lab studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats. But the definition of gain of function covers both general research and especially risky experiments to enhance the ability of potential pandemic viruses to spread or cause severe disease in humans. Fauci has previously stressed he was using the risky experiment definition and that “it would be molecularly impossible” for those bat virus experiments to have turned into the pandemic virus. Trump, a Republican, last year paused some federally funded gain of function research, and on Tuesday his administration announced new rules to tighten oversight. By Lauran Neergaard and Ali Swenson. Swenson reported from New York. Schertler said a verbal clash between Fauci and Paul at a 2021 hearing triggered “an intense and seemingly pathological course of retribution, revenge and obsession”, by the Kentucky senator toward Fauci.
Paul for years has called for Fauci to be indicted and accused him of lying to Congress about whether the National Institutes of Health funded “gain-of-function” research in Wuhan, China, and of helping cover up the origins of Covid-19.

“Given Senator Paul’s obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution, his repeated slanderous comments about me, and recently his publicly releasing my unredacted personal diary aimed at embarrassing and intimidating me,” Fauci said, “the only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars’.”
“Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion,” Fauci said.
Senator Gary Peters, the committee’s top Democrat, said in his opening statement that the hearing was biased and criticised the investigation for having predetermined conclusions.
“This hearing appears to be a culmination of months of biased and selected efforts by the majority, under the guise of a committee investigation, to basically legitimise a predetermined conclusion that was reached years ago,” Peters said.
“It’s not just what we investigate that matters, but how we conduct that investigation that also matters. One-sided investigations designed to validate predetermined conclusions do not serve the American people, who sent us to actually uncover the truth and to solve problems,” Peters said.
Gain-of-function research is, broadly, work that modifies a pathogen in ways that could make it more transmissible or dangerous, though scientists disagree over how narrowly the term should be defined.
That disagreement is the crux of the Paul-Fauci dispute: Paul says the NIH funded such work in Wuhan and that Fauci lied when he denied it, while Fauci says the research did not meet the government’s formal regulatory definition.
Covid-19 origins
Covid-19‘s origins remain unresolved. The FBI said in 2023 that a leak from a laboratory in the central Chinese city of Wuhan likely caused the pandemic, a claim China said had “no credibility whatsoever”.
The CIA said in January 2025 it had shifted its assessment and concluded a lab leak was likely, but with “low confidence”, while four other US intelligence agencies and the National Intelligence Council believe the virus most likely emerged via natural transmission.
Paul this week published a 1,141-page tranche of Fauci’s pandemic-era diary entries, spanning December 2019 through December 2022.
“Many entries in Fauci’s daily historical account completely undermine the official narrative that Fauci and other public health officials espoused,” he said in a statement.
A fact-check document provided by a representative of Fauci said the diary entries match what he said publicly at the time. He has said since 2021 he kept an “open mind” that Covid-19 could have leaked from a lab, and spoke publicly in early 2020 about asymptomatic transmission and China’s lack of transparency, the very matters Paul says the diary reveals.
Chronicle of Fauci’s media appearances
US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, an anti-vaccine activist and, like Paul, a frequent critic of Fauci, told Fox News on July 27 he handed the files to the senator after finding them on government servers.
Both Kennedy and Paul have signaled Fauci’s testimony could expose him to a perjury charge despite Biden’s preemptive pardon.
Paul has for years pledged to see Fauci imprisoned.
The entries largely chronicle Fauci’s media appearances and fame. A review of his public record provided by a representative of Fauci shows his positions were consistent with the diary.
The Trump administration issued a policy on Tuesday barring federal funding for “dangerous gain-of-function” research, the category at the heart of the Fauci dispute.
In April, former Fauci adviser David Morens was indicted on charges of concealing federal records about research grants and the origins of Covid-19, though Fauci was not charged. Biden preemptively pardoned Fauci in January 2025 to guard against “unjustified and politically motivated prosecutions”. REUTERS

Why is Anthony Fauci testifying before Congress? All you need to know about Rand Paul hearing
Anthony Fauci testified before a Senate committee, where he invoked the Fifth Amendment amidst accusations from Senator Rand Paul.
Former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Director Anthony Fauci returned to Capitol Hill on Wednesday for a closely watched Senate hearing led by Republican Senator Rand Paul, reigniting a years-long dispute over the origins of COVID-19 and government-funded virus research.
However, rather than answering lawmakers' questions, Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination, accusing Paul of running an "unhinged" campaign to see him prosecuted.
The hearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee came after Fauci was subpoenaed to testify by Paul, who has repeatedly accused him of misleading Congress about COVID-19-related research.
Here's what led to the latest hearing and why it has once again put the former top US public health official in the spotlight.
Why is Anthony Fauci testifying before Congress?
Fauci was called to testify before the Senate committee chaired by Paul, one of his most outspoken critics since the COVID-19 pandemic. For years, the Kentucky Republican has alleged that Fauci misled Congress about whether the National Institutes of Health (NIH) funded gain-of-function research involving coronaviruses at the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China.
Paul has repeatedly called for Fauci to be criminally prosecuted, accusing him of lying to Congress about the research. Fauci has consistently rejected those allegations, saying the NIH-funded work did not meet the federal government's regulatory definition of gain-of-function research and that he has testified truthfully before Congress on multiple occasions.
The hearing came just days after Paul released more than 1,100 pages of Fauci's pandemic-era diary entries, claiming they contradicted the public narrative surrounding COVID-19.
Representatives for Fauci disputed that characterization, saying the entries were consistent with his public statements, including that he had kept an open mind about a possible lab leak while emphasizing that no definitive conclusion had been reached.
Why did Fauci invoke the Fifth Amendment?
Rather than answering lawmakers' questions, Fauci told the committee he was invoking his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination on the advice of his attorneys.
In his opening statement, Fauci argued that Paul's repeated public calls for his prosecution and the recent release of his unredacted personal diary left him with little choice but to remain silent.
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this Committee is to get me to say something that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said. He also described Paul's campaign against him as an "unhinged obsession."
Fauci's attorney, David Schertler, defended the former health official, calling Paul's pursuit "an obsessive vendetta" and describing the accusations against Fauci as "false and disgraceful."
What is the dispute over?
At the heart of the long-running dispute is whether NIH-backed research connected to the Wuhan Institute of Virology amounted to gain-of-function research, work that modifies pathogens in ways that could make them more transmissible or dangerous.
Scientists have long disagreed over how narrowly the term should be defined, a disagreement that underpins the clash between Paul and Fauci.
The origins of COVID-19 also remain unresolved. According to Reuters, the FBI has assessed that a laboratory leak is the likely source of the pandemic, while the CIA reached a similar conclusion with "low confidence."
Four other US intelligence agencies and the National Intelligence Council continue to assess that the virus most likely emerged through natural transmission.

sources.news_title: Fauci invokes Fifth Amendment and declines to testify in Republican-led COVID-19 Senate hearing - WSVN 7News | Miami News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Dr. Anthony Fauci on Wednesday repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer dozens of questions from senators in a Republican-led committee hearing about his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The decision, at least for now, shielded Fauci from answering questions that could expose him to accusations of lying under oath. Though he received a pardon in early 2025 from Democratic President Joe Biden, some Republicans pursuing a yearslong campaign for his arrest had suggested he could still face charges for any perjury committed during Wednesday’s hearing.
The scientist, who helped lead the nation’s COVID-19 response, was subpoenaed to testify under oath by Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had an antagonistic relationship with Fauci.
In response to angry, sometimes mocking, questions from Republican senators, Fauci declined to answer more than 100 times, injecting new drama into partisan divides that have festered for years about the origins and handling of the pandemic. Fauci himself has become a polarizing figure, even receiving death threats that prompted him to seek security.
In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution.”
“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, behind bars, unquote.” Fauci said, adding that while it pained him to do so, he was following his attorney’s advice by taking the Fifth.
Republicans accuse Fauci of lying while Democrats say he didn’t deserve that
In the combative hearing, Paul and other Republicans accused Fauci of lying in earlier testimony about the origins of the coronavirus, something the longtime National Institutes of Health scientist has forcefully denied. Democrats called the hearing a politically motivated attempt at entrapping Fauci and praised the scientist for his work during the pandemic.
With Fauci declining to answer questions throughout, Paul dominated the approximately three-hour hearing, listing a litany of accusations and detailed questions.
“Today will be the capstone to Anthony Fauci’s 40 years of abuse of power at NIH,” Paul said. “History will judge, but the facts as we now know them paint a sordid tale of dishonesty, misjudgment and ultimately the hubris, the likes of which the world has never seen.”
In one heated moment of the hearing, Paul ejected Fauci attorney David Schertler from the room after he tried to speak without being recognized. In a statement, Schertler said the removal was “outrageous and demonstrates the completely biased and baseless nature of this proceeding.” In another statement, he called Paul’s accusations about Fauci “false and disgraceful.”
Democratic senators praised Fauci and said he didn’t deserve the treatment he was getting.
“This hearing is designed to entrap you,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire.
Paul has long argued Fauci should be criminally investigated based on his belief that the scientist was dishonest in previous testimony to Congress.
The senator announced late in the hearing that the committee would vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt for declining to answer questions. He did not say whether he would push for a criminal contempt referral to federal prosecutors or another charge. He also raised questions about whether Fauci’s pardon affects his eligibility for Fifth Amendment protections.
Paul released some of Fauci’s diary
Leading up to the hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary covering the pandemic years. Pointing to some notes about early efforts at understanding how the virus emerged, Paul said on social media that what Fauci “wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories.”
Some of the diary entries – including Fauci’s uncertainty in the pandemic’s earliest days as scientists around the world raced to understand the new virus and how best to curb it before vaccines could be created – already were reflected in a 2024 memoir and in interviews at the time.
But they have nonetheless drawn attention from people who blame Fauci for mask mandates, school closures and other policies they believe infringed on their rights as hundreds of thousands of people were dying.
Earlier Wednesday, President Donald Trump wrote on social media that he stopped relying on Fauci over the course of the pandemic because he felt the scientist made bad decisions on masks, shutdowns and other issues.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist before entering public office, said on social media that his department found the diary entries in government property and gave them to the committee.
Dozens of disease experts defend Fauci
Scientists also scrambled to Fauci’s defense ahead of the unusual hearing — the second time he has been back before Congress to discuss pandemic origins since leaving the government in 2022. While the COVID-19 pandemic introduced him to millions of Americans, he talked the nation through numerous outbreaks over decades, including HIV, Ebola and the 2001 anthrax attacks, while advising seven presidents.
In a public letter, more than 150 infectious-disease experts and other scientists wrote that “no credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges” and that they are “urging our elected representatives in Congress stop these witch-hunts.”
Among topics discussed at Wednesday’s hearing was whether NIH-funded research in China may have played a role in how the pandemic started.
Many scientists believe the virus most likely emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people, coming to light when it spread at a wildlife market in the Chinese city of Wuhan. There’s no new scientific information supporting that the virus might instead have leaked from a laboratory, a theory Paul champions. A GOP-led subcommittee that studied the question in 2024 did not find any evidence linking Fauci to wrongdoing.
Fauci has long said publicly that he was open to both theories but that there’s more evidence supporting COVID-19’s natural origins.
Republicans also have accused Fauci of lying about whether his agency funded what’s known as gain of function research — the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impact — at a lab in Wuhan.
The NIH for years gave grants to a New York nonprofit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to work with a Chinese lab studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats. But the definition of gain of function covers both general research and especially risky experiments to enhance the ability of potential pandemic viruses to spread or cause severe disease in humans. Fauci has previously stressed he was using the risky experiment definition and that “it would be molecularly impossible” for those bat virus experiments to have turned into the pandemic virus.
Trump, a Republican, last year paused some federally funded gain of function research, and on Tuesday his administration announced new rules to tighten oversight.

Former top US Covid expert Fauci declines to answer hostile Senate questioning
Washington (United States) (AFP) – The former top US infectious disease official on Wednesday faced adversarial questioning from Republican senators about the origins of Covid-19, and on the advice of lawyers invoked his constitutional right not to answer, casting the hearing as a character assassination.
Issued on: Modified:
It was the latest twist in the long-running feud between Anthony Fauci, who spent decades as the nation's top expert in infectious disease, and Republican Senator Rand Paul, who insists on unsubstantiated claims that the origins of the pandemic began in a lab and were covered up.
Paul had subpoenaed the now-retired Fauci to testify before the committee, and prior to the hearing released thousands of pages of the immunologist's personal diary.
Citing Paul's "obsession" with him, Fauci said he would invoke the Fifth Amendment, refraining from answering questions to avoid self-incrimination, adding that it "pains me to do so."
Fauci indicated his lawyers believed Paul intended to entrap him in a slip-up that could result in perjury charges.
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote 'behind bars,'" Fauci said.
Fauci, 85, noted in his opening statement that he had testified before Congress more than 200 times over nearly four decades, saying "I proved that I believe in and respect the value of legitimate congressional oversight."
'Vendetta'
Paul opened with a tirade against Fauci, repeating accusations that under Fauci's watch at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, the US funded so-called "gain-of-function" research in China that triggered the spread of Covid-19.
The senator insists Fauci lied about that to Congress, which he has repeatedly denied.
More than six years after the pandemic's onset, the debate over whether Covid-19 leaked from a lab remains intense. Fauci has maintained that the virus had natural origins, even if he's said he is open to the idea of a lab leak.
Some panel lawmakers criticized the proceedings, including Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan, who said the hearing was designed to "entrap" Fauci.
Paul warned Fauci of "repercussions" for his use of the Fifth Amendment. When Fauci's lawyer attempted to speak on his client's behalf, Paul ordered him removed.
As the approximately three-hour long hearing closed Paul said the committee would vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress for invoking the Fifth, a process that could open increasingly complicated legal puzzles, not least given former President Joe Biden's preemptive pardon of the government scientist.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal meanwhile called the proceedings the result of a "vendetta" and that use of the Fifth must be "respected."
Law professor Tracey Maclin of the University of Florida dubbed "nonsensical" any notion that staying silent was a bad look.
"If his lawyers told him to take the Fifth, that's what he should do," Maclin told AFP, emphasizing that invoking the right was not at all an indication of guilt.
Ahead of the doctor's appearance, a group of more than 150 scientists, physicians and public health activists signed an open letter calling on lawmakers to "stop the on-going vilification and harassment" of scientists, while denouncing "absurd" accusations against Fauci.
Celebrities, Trump and public pressure
US President Donald Trump weighed in on Truth Social, saying Fauci's "ideas were CRAZY!" in the pandemic's early days and accusing him of "trying to protect China."
Fauci's diary excerpts don't offer clear evidence regarding Covid's origins. Rather, the text depicts Fauci grappling with the escalating public health crisis as scientific hypotheses were rapidly evolving.
The journal also offers a glimpse into his deteriorating relationship with Trump, whom he advised during the president's first term.
"Trump getting out of control in pushing to open up the country and get the economy back before election day," Fauci wrote in a passage dated May 2020. "He is desperate. This is all about reelection."
The diary traces Fauci's overnight fame, which thrust him into the spotlight as a lifelong bureaucrat-turned-star who enjoyed attention from celebrities.
But he also details pressures that his day job and his notoriety carried.
"The vicious assault on me continues," Fauci wrote on June 6, 2021. "The entire extreme right wing Republican group in the House and Senate have completely sold their soul to the infinitely lying ex-president trump."

The central focus of the hearing was whether research funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in China contributed to the origins of COVID-19.

sources.news_title: Fauci Repeatedly Invokes the Fifth at Rand Paul’s COVID Hearing
sources.text:
Former infectious disease official Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions in a contentious Wednesday morning hearing held by his outspoken critic, Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, repeatedly invoking the Fifth Amendment.
In his opening statement, Fauci told the Senate Committee on Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs that he believed Paul had an “unhinged obsession” with jailing him, and the only reason he was holding the hearing was to try to catch Fauci in a lie.
“Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said.
Despite the witness’s lack of cooperation, Paul proceeded with questioning Fauci. The senator has long pushed theories that the COVID-19 virus emerged from a lab in China, and that Fauci was aware of this — and knowingly funding risky infectious disease work at the Chinese lab in question. Most scientists agree that the pandemic originated from a natural source, probably a wild animal.
Trending
As promised, Fauci refused to answer any questions.
“On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution,” he said repeatedly in his light Brooklyn drawl.
Paul said following the hearing that he would move to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress for his refusal to answer questions.
“All he had to do today was be honest. If he was honest, even about committing a crime, he would have no jeopardy,” Paul said. “There will be a vote, or at least we’re planning for a vote next week on contempt.”
Courts have previously upheld a witness’s right to invoke the Fifth Amendment in response to a congressional subpoena if they fear self-incrimination. In recent history, the former CEO of ActBlue and a former Biden aide have also declined to answer questions in hearings.
At one point, Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, attempted to address the committee. Paul had security remove him from the hearing room. Many members of the audience applauded his removal as he left.
In a written statement provided to NOTUS, Schertler said that the circumstances surrounding the hearing, including Paul’s repeated calls for Fauci’s imprisonment and the “foreseeable result of these outlandish statements” — including harassment and death threats towards Fauci and members of his family — “regrettably made his continued cooperation impossible.”
“The accusations that Chairman Paul continues to propagate are false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable,” Schertler said in the statement.
Paul and others who opposed the federal government’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic have repeatedly called for Fauci’s imprisonment. In response, former President Joe Biden issued Fauci a preemptive pardon before leaving office.
Paul’s frustration with Fauci was apparent even before the former health official revealed his strategy.
“Frankly, the American people deserve an apology,” Paul told Fauci in his opening statement as chair of the committee.
“That loss of trust may be your most damaging legacy,” Paul said, speaking from a teleprompter. Fauci led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1984 until 2022 and played a key role in the global fight against AIDS as well as COVID-19.
The hearing took place in one of the smaller Senate hearing rooms. Many of the seats were reserved for guests of Paul’s committee. Included in the audience was Mary Holland, CEO of Children’s Health Defense, a vaccine-skeptical organization formerly led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
“Ladies and gentlemen, I’m going to have to ask you to put two masks on,” a man sitting in a committee-reserved seat said jokingly to his neighbors before the hearing began.
It’s the culmination of a frenetic week for both Paul and Fauci. On Tuesday, Paul published excerpts from Fauci’s diary from the pandemic years, claiming that he orchestrated a cover-up of the fact that the pandemic originated in a lab and was the result of so-called “gain-of-function” research, or laboratory work on infectious diseases that makes them more dangerous to humans.
Soon after the release of the diary excerpts, the Trump administration released new guidance prohibiting federal funding going to what it deems gain-of-function research. Scientists have raised concerns that overly broad restrictions could disrupt important research into infectious diseases.
Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), another Fauci critic, attempted to question Fauci on whether the pulmonary infarction he wrote about in the released diary could have been caused by the COVID-19 vaccine. Johnson has repeatedly claimed that the federal government suppressed evidence of dangerous side effects caused by the vaccine.
In contrast to Paul’s threats of repercussions, one Republican appeared to affirm Fauci’s right to decline to answer questions. Like Paul, Sen. James Lankford (R-Oklahoma) attempted to question Fauci on whether the virus originated from a lab. But Lankford responded, “as is your right to do,” when Fauci invoked his right to not answer the question.
Democrats on the committee apologized to Fauci for his being compelled to appear.
“We are here in an attempt to entrap you,” Sen. Margaret Wood Hassan (D-New Hampshire) said during her questioning period, in which she did not actually ask Fauci any questions.
Gary Peters (D-Michigan), the ranking member of the committee, accused Paul of ignoring the actual duties of the committee in favor of promoting his theories around COVID-19.
He pointed to cuts to the public health agencies as the more pressing issue at hand.
“Instead of focusing on the national security challenges that we are facing in our country right now, today’s hearing looks backwards, revisiting questions this committee has already examined,” Peters said. “History tells us, unfortunately, another pandemic is all but inevitable. The question is whether Congress and this committee will work to better prepare our country for it, or continue looking backward while our public health infrastructure crumbles around us.”

sources.text:
Why Anthony Fauci invoked Fifth Amendment at Covid-19 Senate hearing
The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution protects individuals from being compelled to testify against themselves in criminal cases. Invoking the Fifth does not amount to an admission of guilt.
Anthony Fauci, the former Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), attends a US Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, July 29, 2026. (REUTERS)
Former US infectious disease expert Dr Anthony Fauci on Wednesday invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and declined to answer questions before a Republican-led Senate committee investigating his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic. The move came during a hearing chaired by Senator Rand Paul, one of Fauci’s most outspoken critics, and is likely to intensify the long-running political battle over the origins of the coronavirus and federal funding of virus research.
Why did Fauci invoke the Fifth Amendment?
In his opening statement, Fauci said he was acting on the advice of his lawyers because he believed the hearing was part of an effort to prosecute him rather than uncover new facts.
“Under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the 5th Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci told the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. He accused Paul of pursuing an “unhinged” campaign to see him imprisoned and argued that the hearing was intended to get him to say something that could be used against him.
Fauci’s attorney, David Schertler, described Paul’s actions as an “obsessive vendetta” and called the accusations against his client “false and disgraceful.”
🚨 BREAKING: Sen. Rand Paul just had Capitol Police EJECT Anthony Fauci’s attorney from the building after he REFUSED to stop screaming during the hearing
The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution protects individuals from being compelled to testify against themselves in criminal cases. Invoking the Fifth does not amount to an admission of guilt. Instead, it allows a witness to refuse to answer questions if the responses could potentially be used in a future criminal proceeding.
Fauci’s decision means he declined to respond to lawmakers’ questions during Wednesday’s hearing while preserving his constitutional protection against self-incrimination.
Fauci has consistently denied those allegations, saying he testified truthfully before Congress and that the research in question did not meet the government’s regulatory definition of gain-of-function research.
The dispute centres on NIH grants awarded to EcoHealth Alliance, a US-based nonprofit that collaborated with researchers studying bat coronaviruses in Wuhan. While Paul argues the work amounted to gain-of-function research, Fauci maintains it did not fall under the federal definition of experiments considered especially risky.
Covid-19 origins remain unresolved
The hearing also revived debate over how the coronavirus pandemic began.
According to the Reuters report, US intelligence agencies remain divided. The FBI has assessed that a laboratory leak in Wuhan is the likely origin of the virus, while the CIA earlier this year shifted to a “low confidence” assessment favouring the lab-leak theory. Four other US intelligence agencies and the National Intelligence Council continue to believe the virus most likely emerged through natural transmission from animals to humans. China has rejected the lab-leak theory.
Story continues below this ad
Fresh developments
The hearing came days after Paul released more than 1,100 pages of Fauci’s pandemic-era diary entries, arguing they contradicted the government’s public messaging. Fauci’s representatives, however, said the entries were consistent with his public statements throughout the pandemic.
It also followed the Trump administration’s announcement on Tuesday that it would bar federal funding for what it described as “dangerous gain-of-function” research, an issue that has remained at the centre of the years-long dispute between Fauci and congressional Republicans.

sources.news_title: Fauci Pleads the Fifth at Senate Hearing on COVID
sources.text:
Dr. Anthony Fauci, the longtime infectious disease expert who helped lead the federal government's response to the COVID pandemic, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination on Wednesday, refusing to answer questions at a Senate hearing that Republicans had hoped would expose him to potential perjury charges and discredit his handling of the nation's pandemic response.
Appearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, the panel's Republican chairman and one of Fauci's most persistent critics, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases declined to answer questions just minutes into the hearing, saying Paul had made clear his goal was to seek his prosecution.
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said in his opening statement. He accused Paul of having an "obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution" and said the Senator's release of his personal pandemic diary was intended to intimidate and embarrass him.
"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect that I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress," Fauci said, "under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions."
The hearing marked a dramatic moment in the yearslong political battle over the pandemic. Fauci, who advised seven presidents and became the nation's most recognizable public health official during COVID, has appeared before Congress hundreds of times over four decades; Wednesday was the first time he invoked the Fifth Amendment.
The infectious disease expert has been a primary target of Republicans' continuing effort to revisit the government's response to the pandemic and the disputed origins of the coronavirus, issues that have remained central to conservative criticism of Fauci years after he left government service in 2022. Paul and other Republicans have long alleged that the National Institutes of Health funded so-called gain-of-function research at the Wuhan Institute of Virology that contributed to the pandemic, an accusation Fauci has consistently denied. Fauci has maintained that, under the government's definition of gain-of-function research, NIH did not fund such work related to the virus that caused COVID. Federal reviews have not reached a definitive conclusion about the virus's origin, and there is no evidence it was engineered and leaked from a laboratory.
Former President Joe Biden gave Fauci a preemptive pardon in the final hours of his Administration in an effort to protect him from politically motivated charges. But Paul, who has repeatedly accused Fauci of misleading Congress about federally funded virus research in China and the origins of COVID, argued the hearing was necessary regardless. "A pardon that protects a person from criminal prosecution doesn't rewrite history," the Kentucky Senator said in his opening statement. "It does not erase documents. It does not convert a misleading statement to a truthful one, and it does not prevent Congress from establishing what happened."
Ahead of Wednesday's hearing, Paul released roughly 1,100 pages from Fauci's pandemic-era diary, arguing the documents showed discrepancies between Fauci's private thinking and his public testimony.
As Paul pressed ahead with questions despite Fauci's refusal to testify, the former health official responded each time with the same statement: "On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution."
At one point, Paul remarked, "Let the record record that the witness has refused to answer whether there's a folder in front of him based on his Fifth Amendment right."
The hearing also unfolded amid mounting pressure from Trump Administration officials to revisit Fauci's testimony under oath. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said earlier this week that Fauci could face perjury charges if he lied during the hearing despite Biden's preemptive pardon, arguing, "There are many things that (Fauci) said that we know are lies," and adding that "if he lies again, then he could be subject to perjury prosecution."
President Donald Trump likewise weighed in before the hearing, saying on Truth Social that Fauci "made too many bad calls" during the pandemic and asserting that he "didn't let (Fauci) shut the Country down." Trump has repeatedly criticized Fauci's recommendations on masks, shutdowns, and other public health measures.
Biden's pardon shielded Fauci from federal prosecution over actions and testimony connected to his government service during the pandemic. But Republicans have argued that any false statements made in new testimony could expose him to fresh legal jeopardy, a possibility Paul openly discussed before the hearing.
Asked this week about concerns that the hearing was designed to lure Fauci into committing perjury, Paul dismissed the criticism. "There's no risk to perjury if you tell the truth," he told reporters. "The only thing he can't do is lie again."
Democrats criticized the hearing as a partisan exercise. Senator Gary Peters of Michigan, the committee's top Democrat, argued the panel should be focusing on current national security threats rather than revisiting disputes over the pandemic. "Instead of focusing on the national security challenges that we are facing in our country right now, today's hearing looks backwards," Peters said at the hearing. "Rather than building on that work to strengthen our preparedness against future disasters, we are instead relitigating the past."

sources.news_title: Anthony Fauci Pleads Fifth, Declines To Answer Rand Paul's Questions In COVID-19 Hearing
sources.text:
Dr. Anthony Fauci opened his five minutes of testimony Wednesday at a hearing on the origins of COVID-19 by invoking the Fifth Amendment and then declining to answer any of Sen. Rand Paul’s (R-Ky.) questions.
“On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution,” Fauci said in replying to Paul’s questions.
In his opening statement minutes earlier, Fauci said he had testified before Congress multiple times across his 38 years as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, and sat for sworn hearings and dayslong interviews on the same pandemic questions now before the committee.
He added that he would invoke his Fifth Amendment rights due to what he described as Paul’s “obsession” with prosecuting him, pointing to Paul’s repeated calls for him to end up “behind bars,” Paul’s “slanderous comments,” and the senator’s recent release of his unredacted personal diary that Fauci said was intended to embarrass and intimidate him.
“Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion,” Fauci said.
The hearing quickly turned contentious when, minutes into questioning, the senator called on Capitol Police to escort Fauci’s attorney David Schertler from the room for trying to explain why his client was invoking the Fifth. Paul repeatedly told him he wasn’t authorized to speak in the hearing.
“Dr. Fauci has a valid Fifth Amendment privilege and he has the right to assert it. That’s what I was trying to tell the committee,” Schertler told reporters after exiting the hearing room.
Paul grew increasingly frustrated while grilling Fauci, who repeated his Fifth Amendment right and suggested there would be “repercussions” for refusing to respond to his questions.
“The chairman has denied your assertion of privilege and directed you to answer, but you nonetheless refuse and stand on privilege despite the existence of the pardon,” the senator said.
“The committee will have to consider after this hearing what appropriate action should be taken against you for the failure to testify after being directed to do so,” he added. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress. There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”
Fauci, the infectious disease scientist who helped lead the nation’s COVID-19 pandemic response, has become a target of many Republicans’ criticism over his handling of the pandemic, from mask and vaccine mandates to his early public statements on the virus’s origins.
The hearing of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, however, is part of Paul’s yearslong accusations that Fauci lied about the pandemic, a claim Fauci has persistently denied and called “preposterous.”
At the beginning of the hearing, Fauci declined to answer the litany of questions from Paul, who has repeatedly called for him to be criminally prosecuted, and other Republicans so far have expressed skepticism toward public health experts and sweeping government pandemic responses. Democrats, including ranking member Gary Peters (D-Mich.), sought to defend Fauci and cast the hearing as a politicized inquiry.
During the pandemic, Fauci served as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, a role he held since 1984, and, starting in January 2021, also as chief medical adviser to then-President Joe Biden. He retired in 2022, and was later preemptively pardoned by Biden to protect him from potentially politically motivated charges.
The hearing began at 8:30 a.m. ET. Watch here.

sources.news_title: Anthony Fauci invokes fifth amendment and declines to testify in US Senate Covid hearing
sources.text:
Dr Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions at a high-profile Senate committee hearing on the origins of Covid-19 and accused the Republican senator leading questioning of having an “unhinged obsession” with him.
Fauci, the veteran former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), served as a key adviser to Donald Trump and Joe Biden during the Covid-19 pandemic. The hearing was called by Republican Kentucky senator Rand Paul, who has investigated Fauci for years.
Fauci said Paul’s goal was “embarrassing and intimidating me”, and ultimately landing him “behind bars”.
“Therefore, although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of co-operating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys I will invoke my right under the fifth amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said in his opening statement.
Paul, frustrated, later told reporters that he would hold a vote to hold Fauci in contempt of US Congress next week, and described the question of whether the fifth amendment could shield him as “a question for the courts”.
Fauci (85), served under seven US presidents and through numerous health crises, including the HIV crisis, Ebola outbreaks and the first coronavirus outbreak, called Sars-CoV-1. He became a household name overnight when the Covid-19 pandemic halted social life in 2020.
Quickly after opening statements, the hearing became a back-and-forth between Paul and Fauci. Paul grew visibly agitated as Fauci refused to answer, threatened the scientists with “repercussions”, and then tossed one of Fauci’s attorneys from the hearing room.
“Did the [National Institutes of Health] ever fund gain-of-function [research] on monkey pox?” Paul asked, in reference to research that manipulates viruses to make them more effective to shed light on how outbreaks happen.
“On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution,” said Fauci.
After another description of research Paul found unacceptable: “Dr Fauci, did the NIH ever conduct research for or in co-ordination with any element of the intelligence community, CIA, [Office of the Director of National Intelligence]?”
Fauci responded: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.”
Paul pressed on: “Dr Fauci, would you at least like to answer this one question for us today, and let us know whether or not you have changed your mind on whether or not the benefits of gain-of-function [research] outweigh the risks?”
Fauci replied: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the fifth amendment of the constitution.”
A visibly frustrated Paul soon scolded Fauci: “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”
Soon, an attorney for Fauci attempted to join him at the table, and Paul demanded the attorney move.
“This is not a game with his lawyers,” said Paul, to the attorney who was apparently trying to speak, but could not be heard for lack of a microphone. “The attorneys were not recognised.”
“There’s a row behind you, sir,” said Paul. “This is the way Anthony Fauci wants to be remembered – for a lawyer not recognising the rules ... Security please remove him from the room,” Paul said. The attorney patted Fauci on the shoulder and voluntarily left, alongside a guard.
Members of the audience, which conspicuously included rightwing media figure Laura Ingraham, applauded.
In part, Paul’s frustration at the hearing stemmed from a presidential pardon Fauci received from Biden, which in turn implicates the fifth amendment.
There is debate among experts about how far the fifth amendment extends. Some argue that once a person accepts a presidential pardon, they cannot invoke the fifth amendment for federal crimes.
Without that right, Congress could hold a witness in contempt, which can lead to fines or – in the extreme – jail time. Others have argued that the right extends as long as there is a valid threat of prosecution, particularly by states.
“You don’t have any rights under the fifth amendment,” claimed Republican senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, in a line of accusatory questioning. “This is about contempt – contempt for this body, and contempt for the American people.”
Democrats, meanwhile, defended Fauci. Paul is “single-mindedly fixated on seeing Dr Fauci prosecuted for imaginary crimes, and you are so invested in that outcome you have created a personal brand around it”, Fauci’s attorneys argued in a statement read aloud by the Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal, of Connecticut.
In advance of the hearing, Republicans characterised their work as investigating “the origins of Covid-19 and risky taxpayer-funded life science research”, while scientists have characterised the investigation as “vilification and harassment” of Fauci, who led Niaid for 38 years before retiring in 2022. – Guardian

‘Unhinged Obsession’: Fauci Hearing Goes Off the Rails After He Stonewalls Senators
sources.text:
‘Unhinged Obsession’: Fauci Hearing Goes Off the Rails After He Stonewalls Senators
Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right to refuse questions from lawmakers during a high-profile hearing today before the Senate’s Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC). The move has already infuriated Republicans, particularly Committee Chair Rand Paul, who announced before the hearing closed that they will move to attempt to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress.
Republicans, as they have in the past, were set to grill the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) and leader of America’s Covid-19 response on myriad conspiratorial claims about the pandemic.
In his opening statement, Fauci, who has appeared before multiple congressional bodies in the past, told the committee that given Paul’s “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution,” the “only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up — in his words — ‘behind bars.’
“Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion,” he added. “Therefore although it pains me to do so — because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress — under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions.”
Throughout Paul’s questioning, Fauci repeatedly deferred to his constitutional right to refuse the senator’s questions. Before handing off the line of questioning to the committee, Paul berated Fauci and threatened him with consequences.
“The committee will have to consider after this hearing what appropriate action should be taken against you for the failure to testify after being directed to do so,” Paul said. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress. There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.” At the end of the hearing, Paul told the committee that Fauci was not protected by Fifth Amendment privilege in the context of the hearing, and that the committee had “scheduled a vote next week on a resolution certifying your contempt.”
Fauci refused to answer questions, but he was required to sit until dismissed by lawmakers, and the hearing quickly became a mess of grandstanding and theatrics. Paul had one of Fauci’s attorneys removed from the hearing room after he attempted to sit next to Fauci at the witness table, and didn’t heed Paul’s directives to be quiet.
In another tense moment, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) angrily asked Fauci “who the fuck” he thought he was, after referencing a story about a mom who was arrested after attempting to attend a high school football game at the height of the lockdowns. Moreno claimed that that story had motivated him to run for office, saying he could not “stand idly on the side and watch this happen,” and called Fauci a “megalomania” and a disgrace, demanding Fauci apologize.
Fauci has long been a target of not just Paul, but Donald Trump and much of the Republican right, who continue to espouse theories about Covid-19 — from claims that Fauci himself funded the development of the disease to accusations that he is personally responsible for the deaths of millions and the censorship of pandemic-era disinformation about the virus.
The president has long been calling for Fauci and other Joe Biden-era officials to be investigated or prosecuted, and revoked security details for many of his perceived political enemies upon retaking the White House.
This morning, just before the hearing, Trump attempted to shrug off his own role in the pandemic response, writing on Truth Social that “many more people died of Covid under the Biden Administration than under the Trump Administration.”
“I Inherited Fauci, who was there since the 1980’s, but with each passing day, relied less and less on him. He made too many bad calls, like on MASKS … In any event I didn’t let him shut the Country down, although he wanted to. I went the Federalist way, and let the governors decide. The Republican governors did a much better job than the Dumocrats,” Trump wrote. “Biden went on to give Fauci vast destructive power. The rest is history!”
In 2025, as he prepared to leave office, Biden issued a blanket pardon to Fauci and other public officials who were in the crosshairs of the incoming Trump administration. “The issuance of these pardons should not be mistaken as an acknowledgment that any individual engaged in any wrongdoing, nor should acceptance be misconstrued as an admission of guilt for any offense,” the former president wrote. “Our nation owes these public servants a debt of gratitude for their tireless commitment to our country.
“These are exceptional circumstances, and I cannot in good conscience do nothing,” Biden added. “Baseless and politically motivated investigations wreak havoc on the lives, safety and financial security of targeted individuals and their families.”
The pardon, so far, has protected Fauci from any abuses of the Justice Department under Trump, but it can do nothing to stop Republicans from hauling him before Congress.

sources.news_title: Anthony Fauci refuses to answer questions during US Senate hearing about Covid origins
sources.text:
Anthony Fauci refuses to answer questions during tense US Senate hearing about Covid origins
Former top US health official Anthony Fauci has refused to answer questions at a tense US Senate hearing on Covid-19, saying he feared Republicans would try to use his testimony to prosecute him for perjury.
He invoked the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution, which says nobody can be "compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself".
Contradicting himself under oath could be legally perilous for him. Fauci noted he had testified about Covid and its origin at several congressional hearings.
Republicans have long accused Fauci of concealing information about the pandemic from the public and lying about its dangers. He has denied wrongdoing.
Fauci has called the allegations against him "simply preposterous" in previous testimony to lawmakers.
"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government... under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the constitution to refrain from answering your questions," said, Fauci, 85, former leader of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), at Wednesday's hearing.
Taking the Fifth is not an admission of guilt - it is designed to protect individuals against coercion, mistakes, and unfair shifting of the burden to provide proof of wrongdoing.
While he was granted a pre-emptive pardon by former President Joe Biden, protecting him from federal prosecution for his actions between 2014-25, Fauci could still face charges for anything after that date, including in his actions towards the Senate committee. He could also face state or local charges.
In his statement to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security on Wednesday, Fauci said Republican Senator Rand Paul, who chaired the hearing, had an "obvious obsession" with prosecuting him and that had led Fauci to decline to answer questions.
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something - anything - that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said.
Paul, who worked as an eye surgeon before joining Congress, continued questioning Fauci despite his refusal to answer. The Kentucky senator repeatedly invited Fauci to "apologise" and said the committee would vote next week on a resolution holding him in contempt of Congress.
Republicans asked Fauci about shifting health guidance, which changed during the pandemic as health officials learned more about the disease. Fauci has previously defended his policy positions.
One of Fauci's lawyers, David Schertler, who was sitting next to him, repeatedly tried to interject during Paul's questioning and was removed from the room.
Schertler later called it "outrageous" for Paul to "exclude his counsel for making a legitimate legal point".
"It proves the baseless and vindictive nature of this proceeding and Rand Paul's personal vendetta against Dr Fauci," Schertler added in a statement.
During the hearing, President Donald Trump took to social media to call Fauci "crazy".
"I said from the beginning that the Virus came from the Wuhan Laboratory in China. Fauci strongly disagreed, always trying to protect China," Trump said.
The origins of the pandemic have been a matter of strong debate in the US, including between Trump, who was in office when it began in 2020, and public health officials, including Fauci.
The pair frequently sparred over the handling of the pandemic, including when Trump suggested unproven treatments.
In the hearing, Paul suggested that while Fauci said publicly that Covid originated naturally, he privately believed the virus originated in a medical lab. The senator has repeatedly promoted the lab-leak theory that Covid came from China's Wuhan Institute of Virology.
The World Health Organization said last year the natural-origin theory - the virus spilling over from animals to people - was the "best supported" idea from available evidence, but that until more information emerges, the matter is "inconclusive".
Earlier this week, Paul released Fauci's pandemic-era diary entries, in which he mused about fame and Covid's origins.
The diary entries reflect openness at the start of the pandemic to two possible theories about Covid's origins - including natural origins and a lab leak - before he appears to become more convinced it had a natural origin.
In one entry from February 2020 discussing a conference call between Covid scientists, Fauci says the doctors did not have "total agreement" about where the virus came from.
Later, he writes he "is almost certain that the virus evolved naturally from a species jump, even though… I keep an open mind about the possibility of a lab leak".
"[J]ust because two alternatives are possible that does not mean that they are equally probable," Fauci wrote.
His decision not to testify upset Republicans, including Senator Ron Johnson, who told Fauci that he planned to push to subpoena him in an effort to require him to answer lawmakers' questions.
Following the hearing's conclusion, Florida's attorney general, a Republican, said he would open an investigation into Fauci.
Several Democrats, meanwhile, came to Fauci's defence, including Senator Maggie Hassan, who said the hearing was "designed to entrap" him.
Fauci has faced death threats during and after the coronavirus pandemic. Trump last year removed his security protection.
The former top health official was one of the most trusted members of the US government during its response to the pandemic as scientists were trying to learn about the virus as quickly as possible.
He was not always at loggerheads with the current US president. In 2021, Trump awarded Fauci a presidential commendation for his work on the US Covid vaccine project, known as Operation Warp Speed.

sources.news_title: Anthony Fauci Pleads The Fifth During Highly Anticipated Hearing
sources.text:
Former Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment Wednesday in response to questions from Republican Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic.
“On advice of counsel I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution,” Fauci repeatedly said in response to Paul’s questions during the Senate Homeland Security Committee hearing. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Congressman Who Confronted Fauci Reveals What He Expects From Blockbuster Hill Hearing)
Fauci’s stonewalling threatens the ability of Paul’s investigation to obtain answers about the truthfulness of Fauci’s testimony on gain-of-function research in Wuhan, the relationship between the NIH and the intelligence community, signs of engineering in the COVID genome and his history of championing high- risk virology research.
“It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress and there will be repercussions for your refusal to testify today,” Paul said.
That prompted repeated outbursts by Fauci’s attorney, who was subsequently removed by Capitol Police from the hearing.
Paul said that there will be a vote next week on holding Fauci in contempt of Congress.
“Today will be the capstone of Fauci’s forty years of abuse of power at the NIH,” Paul said. “In the end, Fauci must believe he got away with it. But still, late at night, even the guilty must become anxious, re-running the scenarios in his mind, wondering, latching on to lingering doubts, and worrying, did his actions lead to the largest manmade plague in history?”
Fauci’s refusal to answer questions about ties between his institute and high-risk coronavirus research at the Wuhan Institute of Virology marks a dramatic fall from grace for the man once championed by the corporate press as a pandemic hero.
https://fonts.gstatic.com/s/e/notoemoji/17.0/1f6a8/72.pngFauci lawyer ordered by Rand Paul to be REMOVED from the hearing by security after repeatedly interrupting proceedings. pic.twitter.com/cdSaRHBrlY
— Daily Caller (@DailyCaller) July 29, 2026
Paul pressed Fauci on why he funded a maximum security lab in China despite the national security risks, whether NIH handled classified research for the CIA and other spy agencies and whether the lab in Wuhan had the capacity to splice novel spike genes into SARS-related coronaviruses.
Fauci refused to answer.
Finally, Paul asked whether Fauci still felt that the benefits of gain-of-function research were worth the risks, as he wrote in a 2012 editorial in The Washington Post.
Fauci authored the editorial in response to criticism from biosecurity-minded scientists like Rutgers University microbiologist Richard Ebright and Stanford University microbiologist David Relman about the risks of such work.
Fauci said the work should proceed even if it risked triggering a pandemic. The National Institutes of Health kept funding the work. Paul pressed Fauci on whether that worst case scenario had occurred, but did not get an answer.
“I certainly understand why you needed a pardon. I certainly understand why under the advice of counsel you’re not answering any questions, because I think it would be almost impossible for you to answer truthfully without demonstrating what you did,” said Sen. Ron Johnson.
Johnson asked Fauci about evidence from his diary that he suffered a pulmonary infarction in 2021, but received the same obstructive answer.

sources.news_title: Dr. Fauci invokes 5th Amendment and declines to testify in COVID-19 Senate hearing
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Dr. Anthony Fauci on Wednesday invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer questions from senators in a Republican-led committee hearing about his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The move injects new drama into the lingering tensions between Fauci and Republican lawmakers over his handling of the coronavirus pandemic and accusations he lied about the origins of COVID-19, which he denies.
Fauci was set to answer lawmakers’ questions after being subpoenaed by Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had a fraught relationship with the now-retired infectious-disease expert and led the charge seeking that he testify, again, under oath about his role in containing the pandemic.
Fauci’s decision to invoke the Fifth, at least for now, sidesteps calls for his prosecution if he is caught lying at Wednesday’s hearing, part of a yearslong campaign for his arrest spearheaded by some Republicans in Congress. But it may also further inflame partisan divides that have festered for years about the origins and handling of the pandemic, which was declared by the World Health Organization in March 2020.
Fauci, who helped lead the nation’s COVID-19 response, has become a target of those frustrations. But to his supporters he is an emblem of sound scientific expertise.
In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution.”
“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this Committee is to prompt me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said, adding that while it pains him to do so, he is following his attorney’s advice by taking the Fifth.
Paul releases some of Fauci’s diary
Paul in his opening statement sought to build the case that Fauci helped produce the COVID-19 pandemic by approving funding of research on virus mutations and then covered up his complicity.
“Instead of an apology, you have for years avoided responsibility,” Paul said.
Democratic Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the committee’s ranking member, said that Paul’s hearing was a partisan exercise and that the hearing was looking backward instead of focusing on current national security challenges.
Leading up to the hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary covering the pandemic years. Pointing to some notes about early efforts at understanding how the virus emerged, Paul wrote on the social media platform X that what Fauci “wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories.”
Some of the diary entries – including Fauci’s uncertainty in the pandemic’s earliest days as scientists around the world raced to understand the new virus and how best to curb it before vaccines could be created – already were reflected in a 2024 memoir and in interviews at the time.
But they have nonetheless drawn attention from people who blame Fauci for mask mandates, school closures and other policies they believe infringed on their rights as hundreds of thousands of people were dying.
Ahead of the hearing, President Donald Trump wrote on social media that he stopped relying on Fauci over the course of the pandemic because he felt Fauci made bad decisions on masks, shutdowns and other issues.
In a statement, Fauci’s attorney David Schertler said Paul’s accusations are “false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable.”
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist before he entered public office, said Monday that his department gave the diary entries, which were created on a government computer, to the committee. He told a Fox News Channel host that he thought Fauci might lie before the committee, opening him to perjury prosecution despite his preemptive pardon from then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat.
Scientists scrambled to Fauci’s defense ahead of the unusual hearing — the second time the longtime National Institutes of Health scientist has been back before Congress to discuss pandemic origins since leaving the government in 2022. While the COVID-19 pandemic introduced him to millions of Americans, he talked the nation through numerous outbreaks over decades, including HIV, Ebola and the 2001 anthrax attacks, while advising seven presidents.
Some disease experts criticize the accusations against Fauci
In a public letter, more than 150 infectious-disease experts and other scientists wrote that “no credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges” and that they are “urging our elected representatives in Congress stop these witch-hunts.”
The expected crux of Wednesday’s hearing was whether NIH-funded research in China may have played a role in how the pandemic started.
Many scientists believe the virus most likely emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people, coming to light when it spread at a wildlife market in the Chinese city of Wuhan. There’s no new scientific information supporting that the virus might instead have leaked from a laboratory, a theory Paul champions. A GOP-led subcommittee that studied the question in 2024 did not find any evidence linking Fauci to wrongdoing.
Fauci has long said publicly that he was open to both theories but that there’s more evidence supporting COVID-19’s natural origins, the way other deadly viruses including coronavirus cousins SARS and MERS jumped into people.
Republicans also have accused Fauci of lying about whether his agency funded what’s known as gain of function research — the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impact — at a lab in Wuhan.
The NIH for years gave grants to a New York nonprofit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to work with a Chinese lab studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats. But the definition of gain of function covers both general research and especially risky experiments to enhance the ability of potential pandemic viruses to spread or cause severe disease in humans. Fauci has previously stressed he was using the risky experiment definition and that “it would be molecularly impossible” for those bat virus experiments to have turned into the pandemic virus.
Trump, a Republican, last year paused some federally funded gain of function research, and on Tuesday his administration announced new rules to tighten oversight.
