sources.news_title: Fauci’s testimony could lead to prosecution: Here’s how
sources.text:
Dr. Anthony Fauci, who helped lead the nation’s COVID-19 pandemic response, could trigger a new round of litigation and even expose himself to prosecution despite the sweeping pardon issued by former President Joe Biden.
Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky subpoenaed Fauci to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul chairs, on Wednesday. But at the session, Fauci repeatedly pleaded the Fifth Amendment, accusing Paul of being obsessed with prosecuting him.
Paul has long accused Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), of lying about the pandemic, a charge Fauci has repeatedly denied.
Over the weekend, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary covering the pandemic years. Pointing to some notes about early efforts at understanding how the virus emerged, Paul wrote on X that what Fauci "wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories."
In an earlier letter to Paul, Fauci’s attorneys called his allegations "absolutely baseless" and part of an "obsessive and groundless vendetta."
In another post on X on Tuesday, Paul said if Fauci "comes before my committee tomorrow and perjures himself, his preemptive pardon from former president Joe Biden will not protect him."
Biden issued the pardon for Fauci and others before leaving office last year, as a guard against potential attacks by the incoming Trump administration.
Newsweek has contacted representatives for Fauci and Paul for further comment via emails sent outside regular business hours.
Why Fauci could be in trouble
Constitutional attorney Ross Garber noted in a post on X that the Fifth Amendment applies only when a witness faces a "reasonable fear of prosecution."
Because Biden granted Fauci a full federal pardon for conduct through early 2025, Garber said the Senate could argue that Fauci has no valid basis to invoke the privilege for matters covered by that pardon. According to Garber, the committee has two potential avenues: pursue civil litigation to compel Fauci’s testimony or issue a criminal‑contempt referral to the Justice Department, which could seek an indictment.
Politico's legal reporter Kyle Cheney said on X that Fauci’s strategy carries significant risk. While the pardon shields him from prosecution for past conduct, it does not protect him from future crimes—including perjury or contempt. Cheney said relying on the Fifth Amendment to avoid all questioning could itself become grounds for a contempt case.
Investigative correspondent Catherine Herridge reported on X that former senior Justice Department officials believe there are multiple ways to challenge the validity of Biden’s preemptive pardon.
One approach would involve charging Fauci with a new offense and forcing a court to test the pardon’s scope. Another centers on Congress: because Fauci has theoretically been pardoned for past and future criminal exposure tied to his NIH work, Herridge said lawmakers could argue he has no plausible Fifth Amendment claim at all—and move to compel testimony. A contempt finding could follow.
Herridge also highlighted pressure surrounding Dr. David Morens, Fauci’s longtime senior adviser, who has been indicted on conspiracy and obstruction charges, including destruction and alteration of federal records.
Prosecutors allege Morens used personal email accounts to evade federal transparency laws. Herridge reported that Morens’ legal jeopardy—he has pleaded not guilty—could make him a potential cooperating witness if prosecutors seek leverage in the broader inquiry. During Wednesday’s hearing, Senator Rick Scott raised the Morens case as Fauci continued to invoke the Fifth.
Paul said in an interview with Fox Business earlier this month that if Fauci "lies during the hearing, that’s a new lie, and the pardon won’t cover that."
Fauci's Pardon Under Biden Explained
In one of his final acts as president, Biden issued a preemptive pardon for Fauci in January 2025.
The pardon said it covered any offenses Fauci "may have committed or taken part in during the period from January 1, 2014, through the date of this pardon arising from or in any manner related to his service as Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, as a member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force or the White House COVID-19 Response Team, or as Chief Medical Advisor to the President."
At the time, Biden said the preemptive pardons for Fauci and others should not be "mistaken as an acknowledgment that any individual engaged in any wrongdoing" or that acceptance of them should be "misconstrued as an admission of guilt for any offense."
He said those who were issued pardons "have served our nation with honor and distinction and do not deserve to be the targets of unjustified and politically motivated prosecutions."
Fauci was director of the NIAID at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for nearly 40 years, including during Trump’s term in office, and later served as Biden’s chief medical adviser until his retirement in 2022.
Rand Paul and Dr. Fauci’s History
Paul’s subpoenaing of Fauci is the latest episode in a series of clashes between the pair over the origins of the virus that caused the COVID-19 pandemic.
Paul has long called for Fauci to be indicted and accused him of lying to Congress about whether the NIH funded "gain-of-function" research in Wuhan, China, and of helping cover up the origins of COVID-19.
Fauci has denied both claims and said he has testified truthfully multiple times before Congress on the issues.
"I have not lied before Congress. I have never lied. Certainly not before Congress. Case closed," Fauci told Paul during a 2021 hearing.
"Gain of function" research is the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impact. NIH for years gave grants to a New York nonprofit called EcoHealth Alliance that used some of the funds to work with a Chinese lab studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats.
But the definition of "gain of function" covers both general research and especially risky experiments to "enhance" the ability of potentially pandemic pathogens to spread or cause severe disease in humans. Fauci has previously stressed he was using the risky experiment definition and that "it would be molecularly impossible" for those bat virus experiments to have turned into the pandemic virus.
Fauci Diary Entries
The diary entries released by Paul provide a behind-the-scenes account of the pandemic's earliest months, revealing private debates about the origins of the virus, concerns about Trump's public messaging and sharp disagreements inside the government response.
Some of the diary entries express uncertainty about the origins of COVID-19. The leading theories are that the virus jumped from animals to humans at a market in Wuhan or leaked in a lab incident.
Fauci wrote in an entry on January 26, 2020 that "we know the market was not the source, it was the amplifier," though he added that "somewhere the virus jumped from animals to humans."
In a January 31, 2020 entry, Fauci wrote that Jeremy Farrar, then director of the Wellcome Trust, and several scientists had raised concerns about parts of the virus they believed warranted closer scrutiny.
Fauci wrote that some researchers were focusing on the furin cleavage site—a feature of the virus that helps it infect human cells—as they explored whether the virus could have arisen naturally.
"They bring up the possibility that this could have been deliberately inserted and either accidentally released or deliberately released by a crazy person in the lab," Fauci wrote.
He also noted that during a February 1, 2020 call with U.S. and international health experts, there was disagreement about the origins of the virus.
Some of the entries—including Fauci’s uncertainty in the pandemic’s earliest days as scientists around the world raced to understand the new virus—already were reflected in Fauci’s 2024 memoir and in interviews at the time.
The Likely Flashpoints
The crux of Wednesday’s hearing is expected to be whether NIH-funded research in China may have played any role in how the pandemic started.
Many scientists believe the virus most likely emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people, coming to light when it spread at a wildlife market in Wuhan, China.
There’s no new scientific information supporting the theory that the virus might instead have leaked from a laboratory, a theory Paul champions.
Fauci has long said publicly that he was open to both theories, but that there’s more evidence supporting COVID-19’s natural origins, the way other deadly viruses including coronavirus cousins SARS and MERS jumped into people.
COVID Origins Remain Inconclusive
Official investigations into the origins of the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic remain inconclusive.
An expert group charged by the World Health Organization to investigate the pandemic said in its final report last year that scientists were not sure how the pandemic began. It said most scientific data supports the hypothesis that the virus jumped to humans from animals, though it acknowledged that it was unable to get the necessary data to evaluate whether or not COVID-19 was the result of a lab accident.
The FBI said in 2023 that the virus "most likely" spread after a leak from a lab in Wuhan, which China dismissed. The CIA in 2025 said it believes the virus most likely originated from a laboratory, though the agency acknowledged it has "low confidence" in its assessment.
Four other U.S. intelligence agencies and the National Intelligence Council believe the virus most likely emerged via natural transmission, although that assessment was also made with low confidence.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Robert Greenall

Children lost years of education, small businesses built over a lifetime disappeared, patients delayed cancer screenings and other medical care,… pic.twitter.com/ZY1XCkqvHb
Even though Fauci appeared before the committee, he had no intention of providing substantive testimony.
“Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right, under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution, to refrain from answering your questions. Thank you.”
HAPPENING NOW: Anthony Fauci PLEADS THE FIFTH, refuses to speak on COVID-19 or leaked diary entries.
— Townhall.com (@townhallcom) July 29, 2026
Coward. pic.twitter.com/YpixJgcaSQ
And plead the Fifth, he did — repeatedly.
In fact, Fauci’s efforts to avoid incriminating himself reached an uncanny level of absurdity when he refused to even answer whether there was a red folder in front of him.
"It's a crime under 18 U.S.C. Section 1001 to knowingly make a material false statement to Congress with a penalty up to five years of imprisonment," Paul said. He noted that the CIA, the FBI, and the Department of Energy have all concluded that the virus likely came from the lab in Wuhan, then asked the question Fauci had spent years dodging: "How did you come to the conclusion that a totalitarian country would be capable of doing this in a BSL-2 lab, a lab that lacked the security?" He pressed further, asking whether Fauci regretted the decision and would make the same call today. "Can you explain to the committee why you chose to fund this dangerous research in China?" Paul asked.
Fauci had his answer ready.
"On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution," he said.
Paul tried again. "In the red folder on your table is a copy of Section 192 of Title II of the U.S. Code," Paul said. "Your counsel has been provided a copy as well. That section makes it a crime for a witness appearing under subpoena to refuse to answer any questions pertinent to the question under inquiry. Do you have that in front of you?"
Fauci gave the exact same answer, word for word. “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution.”
So, Fauci literally would not confirm whether a folder existed on the table in front of him without invoking a constitutional right against self-incrimination. Paul let the moment speak for itself. "Let the record record that the witness has refused to answer whether there's a folder in front of him based on his Fifth Amendment right," Paul said.
Fauci REPEATEDLY invokes the Fifth Amendment before Congress pic.twitter.com/vNCVWu3wjP

sources.news_title: 4 takeaways as Fauci pleads the Fifth throughout hearing over COVID origins
sources.text:
4 takeaways as Fauci pleads the Fifth throughout hearing over COVID origins
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Dr. Anthony Fauci repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment when pressed by senators during a hearing over his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic and its origins, accusing the chairman of having an “unhinged obsession” with him and trying to entrap him in questioning.
He appeared before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs committee on Wednesday after being subpoenaed by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., who has led several investigations into Fauci’s handling of the pandemic and National Institutes of Health funding for virus research in China.
Fauci said he had testified more than 200 times over his nearly four decades running the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and that he could not answer questions on the advice of his lawyers.
“Given Sen. Paul’s obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution, his repeated slanderous comments about me, and recently his publicly releasing my unredacted personal diary aimed at embarrassing and intimidating me, the only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said.
Wednesday’s hearing comes after Paul released more than 1,000 pages from Fauci’s personal diary during the pandemic years. For Fauci’s critics, entries in the diary detailing uncertainties about the virus in the early days of the pandemic were evidence he was telling the public a different story than he was writing in private.
PLEADING THE FIFTH
Every question posed to Fauci was met with the invocation of the Fifth Amendment, leaving lawmakers with little new insight to his thinking or actions during the pandemic. Fauci has appeared before congressional panels several times since the outset of the pandemic, that have regularly turned into partisan brawls among lawmakers.
Several Republican lawmakers viewed Fauci’s refusal to answer questions as an admission of guilt and claimed he did not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment because of the pardon granted by former President Joe Biden over concerns he could be targeted by a potentially vindictive prosecution by the Trump administration.
“I certainly understand why, on the advice of counsel, you're not answering any questions because I think it'll be almost impossible for you to answer the questions truthfully without really demonstrating what you did, your culpability,” said Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.
The Fifth Amendment protects individuals from being compelled to provide testimony that could incriminate them. Courts have consistently held invoking the right is not an admission of guilt by itself.
Paul told Fauci there would be consequences for his refusal to answer lawmakers’ questions and that a vote will be held next week on whether to hold him in contempt of Congress.
“It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress,” Paul said. “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”
Democrats accused Republicans of holding the hearing in an attempt to trap Fauci in criminal wrongdoing.
“It is unfortunate that you have been put in the position that you are in today. And it must be enormously frustrating to know that this hearing is designed to entrap you,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H.
COVID’S ORIGINS
The central issue in Paul’s investigation is whether the coronavirus developed naturally or in a laboratory. Paul has alleged the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases funded dangerous “gain-of-function” research in China that got out of control and led to the creation of a virus leading to a global pandemic.
Gain-of-function research involves scientists altering the genetic makeup of viruses to better understand how they evolve and using that information to prevent future pandemics. Such experiments have been controversial among scientists and policymakers for years.
Fauci and other officials have disputed NIH funded gain-of-function research that caused the pandemic and said the grants in question supported other research that didn’t meet the definition of prohibited gain-of-function experiments.
Paul pressed Fauci on what he described as “extensive” support for the research, whether he had directed U.S. funding to it around the world and whether American inspectors had examined Chinese labs. Fauci declined to answer any of the questions and invoked the Fifth Amendment.
“Your primary concern was hiding that fact that you had approved the funding for this dangerous research. Your support for gain-of-function research is extensive and longstanding,” Paul said.
Debate over whether the virus emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people or came from a lab is still prominent years after the pandemic has subsided. Fauci has said he is open to both theories but that there is more evidence supporting a natural origin.
U.S. intelligence agencies have reached differing conclusions about the origin of the virus, and none have reached a definitive conclusion.
ACCUSATIONS OF LIES AND SECRECY
Along with frequent criticisms of his decision to plead the Fifth, Republicans frequently claimed Fauci misled the public compared to what he was writing in his diary and that his direction over lockdowns and other COVID precautions caused widespread harm to Americans.
Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., also pressed Fauci on whether he told the truth in 2024 testimony before Congress, including about his relationship with Dr. David Morens, a former senior adviser at the NIH.
Morens was indicted earlier this year on charges of skirting federal record-keeping laws and accused of concealing emails over the origins of the coronavirus outbreak. Prosecutors accused Morens of working with scientists outside the federal government to protect funding for virus research.
Fauci, who has not been accused of wrongdoing in the case, has tried to distance himself from Morens and told lawmakers in a 2024 hearing that they didn’t work together closely.
Scott asked Fauci whether he had used private email accounts to conduct his government business or whether he ever directed anyone to destroy records related to congressional investigations. Fauci declined to answer, citing the Fifth Amendment.
DEMOCRATS FOCUS ON TRUMP
Several Democratic senators tried to flip the script of the hearing on the Trump administration and its response to the current outbreaks of measles and cyclospora. They also said the administration had undermined public confidence in vaccines and the nation’s public scientists.
“Since January 2025, the Trump administration has taken a number of actions to drastically weaken our ability to fight infectious diseases and biological threats that endanger Americans,” Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., said. “That is something this committee should be looking at.”
They also argued the GOP’s attacks directed toward Fauci will scare people away from wanting to become public servants in the future.
“It’s sending signals to others who are thinking about serving our country, our scientists, our doctors, our healthcare professionals, our researchers trying to show to them that if you don’t get in line with the politics, that you will also potentially be subject to attacks,” Kim said.

sources.news_title: Fauci pleads the Fifth; Rand Paul threatens charges: Live hearing updates
sources.text:
Anthony Fauci pleads the Fifth during Republican questioning on COVID
WASHINGTON – Dr. Anthony Fauci may be held in contempt of Congress after refusing to answer Republicans' questions about the origins of COVID-19, invoking the Fifth Amendment right against incriminating himself during a Senate committee hearing on Wednesday.
Sen. Rand Paul, the Kentucky Republican who for years pushed for answers about the origin of the coronavirus, said a Senate panel will hold a vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt. He said Fauci should have testified because former President Joe Biden issued him a preemptive pardon.
Fauci appeared under subpoena in a hearing so tense that Paul had one of Fauci's attorneys ejected from the room. After reading a statement saying the purpose of the hearing was to entrap him, Fauci repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to otherwise respond to a barrage of questions from Republicans.
Democrats defended Fauci as a doctor who served the public for nearly 40 years as the nation's top virologist. “It must be enormously frustrating to know that this hearing is designed to entrap you,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-New Hampshire, told him.
"Americans are asking for accountability, Dr. Fauci, and your silence is very telling," said Sen. Joni Ernst, a Republican from Iowa.
Top takeaways from the Fauci hearing
Fauci's leadership guiding America through the COVID-19 pandemic came under scathing criticism at Wednesday's hearing, during which he was pilloried by Republicans for invoked his right against self-incrimination.
GOP senators mocked Fauci and spent the morning castigating his response to the pandemic, accusing him of violating the law as he sat stone-faced without rebutting. They keyed on more than 1,100 pages from Fauci's personal diary that the committee released to argue he wasn't telling Americans the truth about COVID-19.
Democrats at the hearing came to Fauci's defense, praising his service and saying the public inquisition was unjustified and an attempt at "entrapment."
Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, has been sharply criticized by many on the right for years, and the hearing encapsulated more than six years of political brawling about pandemic policies.
Read more on the top takeaways from the contentious hearing.
Trump says he watched Fauci hearing, has 'respect' for Biden pardon
Joey Garrison
President Donald Trump said he watched the entire Senate hearing as Fauci declined to answer every question by repeatedly invoking his Fifth Amendment right.
In his first public reaction to Fauci's appearance before a Senate committee, Trump on Wednesday sought to distance himself from the original face of his administration's COVID-19 response, yet did not pile on the 85-year-old former infectious disease director.
"He wasn't a big factor for me. He was a very big factor for Biden," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "COVID was a disaster but Fauci did not help."
A reporter asked Trump why he believes Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment so many times given the blanket immunity he holds from any past criminal from former President Joe Biden's pardon.
"Well, look, I've never been a big fan of Fauci," Trump said. "Why he did that was very simple: His lawyer told him to. I don't know if he would have been better off not doing it. There were a lot of questions that I guess he could have answered, and some maybe he didn't feel comfortable answering."
Asked about the validity of Biden's final-hour pardon for Fauci, Trump seemed to defend it.
"He was pardoned by Biden, and I respect that. I know how powerful it is," Trump said.
Contempt vote creates legal questions
Zachary Schermele
Paul's threat to hold a committee vote on pursuing recommendations for contempt charges against Fauci has already created a cloud of legal questions. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Florida, told USA TODAY he'd support the effort, and that Fauci's decision to plead the Fifth was misguided.
"I think he caused a lot of mistrust," he said.
Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, told USA TODAY she wants to discuss the move further to "really understand the legal ramifications" among other members of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
"I'd want to talk to a general counsel and just understand how we proceed," she said.
Sen. Gary Peters, D-Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel, told reporters after Wednesday morning's hearing that he wasn't "assessing anybody’s legal liability."
"We'll see what happens going forward," he said. "I would hope that we start doing some hearings on actually how we prepare the United States for future pandemics."
Cassidy mum on Fauci hearing
Zachary Schermele
Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Republican chairman of the Senate health committee, said he didn’t watch the Fauci hearing.
Cassidy, a doctor and prominent immunization defender despite vaccine skeptics within his own party, declined to give his thoughts on Fauci’s decision to plead the Fifth.
"I truly didn’t watch it," he told USA TODAY on Wednesday afternoon. "Somebody told me that."
House seeks to question Fauci, too
Bart Jansen
A House committee chairman threatened to subpoena Fauci after a previous secretary of Health and Human Services refused to release his diary, which revealed positions that seemed to conflict with his public statements about the COVID-19 pandemic and response.
Rep. James Comer, R-Kentucky, the head of the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, said former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra refused to turn over the diary when his panel sought it. Current HHS Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. gave the diary to the Senate.
“Dr. Fauci is trapped by the many lies he repeatedly told the American public,” Comer said. “If former President Biden’s blanket autopen pardon is valid, then Dr. Fauci has no right to refuse to answer questions.”
RFK Jr. criticizes Fauci in post
Erin Mansfield
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. shared a post on X, formerly known as Twitter, with a photo of Fauci sitting in the witness chair and a headline saying he was invoking his Fifth Amendment right.
"Dear Diary… If I plead the Fifth, will I still be famous?" the post reads. Kennedy previously told Fox News that his staff, who oversee the offices where Fauci worked, compiled his diaries from files on 11 different servers.
Missed the hearing? Watch a replay here
Fauci departs hearing without answering questions from reporters
Zac Anderson
The hearing ended after roughly three hours of questioning, with Fauci escorted out by police and walking past reporters shouting questions in the hallway without answering.
Sen. Rand Paul, in his closing statement, accused Fauci of "40 years of abuse of power" and declared that "history will judge" his actions.
Senate committee to vote on holding Fauci in contempt
Joey Garrison
The Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs will vote next week on holding Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress for refusing to answer questions at Wednesday's hearing, Sen. Rand Paul said before the hearing ended.
Though Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right to not answer any questions, Sen. Rand Paul, the committee's chairman, argued the privilege is "unsupported" because of the blanket pardon Biden awarded Fauci before leaving office. Paul said the committee's questions for Fauci were only limited to the period covered by Biden's pardon.
Paul also said Fauci waived his Fifth Amendment privilege because of the introduction he gave the committee prior to announcing he would be invoking his Fifth Amendment right.
"I find your objection unsupported and direct you to answer the question," Paul said.
As he did throughout the hearing, Fauci responded by reading off his Fifth Amendment right.
Paul responded by saying the committee has scheduled a vote next week on a resolution holding Fauci in contempt because of his refusal to answer questions.
Paul closes hearing saying Fauci funded research into largest plague in history
Bart Jansen
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, closed the hearing by arguing that Fauci abused his power at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and helped fund research that led to “the largest manmade plague in human history.”
“Today will be the capstone to Anthony Fauci’s 40 years of abuse of power at NIH,” Paul said. “At the end, we must imagine that Fauci believes he got away with it.”
How Sen. Rand Paul obtained Fauci's diary
Joey Garrison
Sen. Rand Paul, who chairs the committee, obtained Fauci's diary entries through a subpoena, according to a spokesperson from the senator's office.
The diary was typewritten, not written by hand, which indicates Fauci chronicled his thoughts on a computer.
Though Fauci referred to the journal as his "personal diary," Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said it was written on a government computer. Kennedy told Fox News that it took about eight months to produce the diary entries from 11 separate government servers.
"We handed them over this week," Kennedy told Fox News this week. In a post on X, Kennedy said, "These were not personal journals. They were government records created on a government computer by a federal employee during one of the most consequential public health emergencies in history."
Paul says 'natural immunity' was better strategy than isolation against COVID-19
Bart Jansen
GOP Sen. Rand Paul said a better strategy for coping with COVID-19 pandemic would have been to rely on “natural immunity” rather than isolating the sick from their relatives or wearing masks.
Paul acknowledged that while smallpox infection provides lifelong immunity, exposure to COVID-19 provides less protection against future infections.
But he said deploying nurses who had recovered from the virus or allowing relatives to congregate if they had all been exposed would have been better than isolating the sick. He said the lesson of “natural immunity” has been known since the Athenian plague of 486 BC.
“We could have used natural immunity as somewhat of a block of protection,” Paul said. “Not something perfect, but a useful tool that could have helped people.”
Fauci invokes 'blanket Fifth' to avoid potential prosecution, legal analyst says
Terry Collins
Fauci is consistently invoking his Fifth Amendment rights at his lawyers’ urging because he thinks answering questions could expose him to the risk of prosecution, a former prosecutor told USA TODAY.
"Fauci is invoking his Fifth because he doesn’t want to be subjected to any possible perjury," said Steven Clark, a former Santa Clara County District Attorney in San Jose, California. "This is not surprising to me. He thinks, 'this is a for-show, gotcha hearing, and I’ve been threatened with criminal prosecution before, and not going to subject myself to the possibility of that.'
"You can’t just pick and choose what questions you will answer; you have to take a blanket Fifth," Clark continued. "He’s playing it very safe, and I think it’s totally understandable, even if the optics aren’t very good.
"There’s a misunderstanding that pleading the Fifth implies that you’re guilty of something, but that’s not the legal standard," Clark concluded. "He’s simply following his lawyers’ advice."
Before leaving office, former President Joe Biden pardoned Fauci for any actions dating back to 2014, but Clark said that doesn't protect Fauci from potential charges based on his actions since then.
"It’s a preemptive pardon that only protects him from past conduct, and not a potential prosecution for perjury that occurs after the pardon was given," Clark said.
Moody highlights “free state of Florida” vs Fauci
Zac Anderson
Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Florida, recounted the fight over COVID restrictions in her state, which emerged as a major battleground.
Moody noted her efforts as Florida attorney general to push back against federal policy and praised Gov. Ron DeSantis, whose COVID pushback grew his national political profile and laid the foundation for a presidential run. Fauci slammed DeSantis in his diary, which Moody read from.
“We fought back. We got ridiculed for it,” Moody said, adding: “We are now called the free state of Florida.”
Democrats on committee leave Fauci hearing
Joey Garrison
As Republican senators on committee hammered Fauci one after another, Democrats eventually walked out.
The Democratic side of the committee table turned completely empty about one hour and 45 minutes into the hearing.
With Fauci invoking his Fifth Amendment right not to answer any questions, Republicans have seized the opportunity to present Fauci with a wide range of criticisms about him and his advice to Americans unchallenged.
Earlier in the hearing, Democratic Sens. Gary Peters of Michigan, Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and John Fetterman of Pennsylvania each spoke. Hassan accused Republicans of seeking to "entrap" Fauci.
But apparently the Democrats on the panel have nothing else they want to say before the hearing ends.
Hawley mocks Fauci taking the Fifth Amendment
Zac Anderson
What day is it? What's your tie color? What's the carpet color?
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Missouri, asked Fauci a series of basic questions that seemed aimed at undercutting his argument for invoking the Fifth Amendment to avoid any legal jeopardy.
Fauci stuck with his standard response, saying: "On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution."
"Nothing says honesty like taking the Fifth, huh, doc?" Hawley began.
Hawley accused Fauci of violating the law and said he's "done more to harm science than anybody in my lifetime."
"I hope you'll go home and write that in your diary," he added.
Republicans target Fauci's legacy: 'This is how history will remember you'
Joey Garrison
Republicans on the committee have used the hearing to air some of their long-held criticisms about Fauci and his medical advice to Americans.
As Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment and refused to answer questions, GOP senators took the opportunity to target the legacy of the infectious disease expert.
"We have entire generations of Americans who, rightfully so, do not trust our institutions to keep them safe because of you," Sen. Rick Scott of Florida told Fauci. "This has destroyed decades of progress and lifetimes of work because you wanted to fuel your own ego and be the center of attention."
"What would you do differently knowing what you know today, Dr. Fauci?" Scott asked,
"On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution," Fauci replied.
"In hindsight, are you disappointed how you handled COVID? Do you have any regrets?" Scott asked in another exchange.
Fauci provided the same answer.
"Your legacy will not be as a man who has saved America from COVID, but as a man who destroyed the public trust in America's public health institutions in exchange for five minutes of fame," Scott said. "This is how history will remember you."
Rick Scott presses Fauci on 2024 testimony
Erin Mansfield
Sen. Rick Scott, R-Florida, pressed Fauci on the truthfulness of statements he made in 2024 testimony before Congress, including about his relationship with an advisor.
Scott also asked whether Fauci ever directed anyone to destroy records related to Congress' investigation, or was aware of anyone who did.
Fauci declined to answer, citing his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.
Why Fauci says he invoked the Fifth Amendment
Joey Garrison
Fauci said he invoked his Fifth Amendment right not to answer any questions at the hearing because of Republican Sen. Rand Paul's "obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution."
Fauci said the hearing has one purpose: entrap him into saying something that could potentially be used against him in court.
Reading from a one-page statement at the beginning hearing, Fauci cited "repeated slanderous comments about me" from Paul, the committee's chairman, and the recent release of Fauci's diary "aimed at embarrassing and intimidating me."
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something ‒ anything ‒ that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars,'" Fauci said.
"Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion," Fauci said. "Therefore ‒ although it pains me to do so because of the respect that I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress ‒ under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions."
Throughout the hearing, Fauci has invoked the Fifth in declining to answer questions posed by Republicans. Democrats on the committee have echoed Fauci's argument that the hearing is meant to entrap him.
Blumenthal accuses hearing of trying to rewrite history
Bart Jansen
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Connecticut, said the COVID-19 pandemic was one of the darkest times in U.S. history, suggesting Wednesday's hearing was part of the Trump administration’s effort to rewrite the history of a pandemic.
The Trump administration launched baseless smears against vaccines that pulled the country out of the crisis that killed 1 million Americans and 15 million worldwide, Blumenthal said. Fauci spent decades in federal government helping “conquer” COVID-19, HIV, swine flu, Zika, Ebola and other epidemics, he said.
“For the past 18 months, the Trump administration has been engaged in a campaign to rewrite this history,” Blumenthal said. “Today’s proceeding, I fear, is part of that effort, one of the darkest days in our Senate’s history.”
Hassan says hearing aims to 'entrap' Fauci
Bart Jansen
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-New Hampshire, thanked Fauci for more than 50 years of federal government service and lamented the spread of public-health crises.
Hassan said the 4,500 cases of measles reported since January 2025 are more than the total from 2020 to 2024 combined. Thousands of people have been sickened by a food-borne parasite that “is nowhere near under control,” Hassan said.
Fauci refused to answer questions at the hearing based on his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination, and Republicans threatened to charge him with obstruction.
“It must be enormously frustrating to know that this hearing is designed to entrap you,” Hassan said.
Fauci fidgets as senators continue questions
Bart Jansen
Fauci moved a pen between his hands and clasped his hands above the witness table as lawmakers such as Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wisconsin, continued to ask questions that he refused to answer.
Fauci sat mute as Johnson described adverse health effects from COVID-19 vaccines and the efficacy of ivermectin to treat the virus.
Johnson accused Fauci of “sabotaging” research on other medications before he again invoked the Fifth Amendment against testifying.
What is the Fifth Amendment?
Erin Mansfield
The Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution protects people from having to incriminate themselves in court, and instead forces prosecutors to prove their case.
Fauci is appearing in front of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Government Affairs under a subpoena and repeatedly reading a statement saying his lawyers advised him to invoke his Fifth Amendment right.
Fauci attorney removed from hearing at Paul's direction
Joey Garrison
Sen. Rand Paul, the committee's chair, ordered security to remove one of Dr. Anthony Fauci's attorneys from the room after the attorney refused to leave the table where Fauci sat.
Paul accused the attorney of speaking out of turn and interrupting proceedings when he tried to intervene on a question posted to Fauci, who has invoked his Fifth Amendment rights throughout the hearing.
"The attorneys are not recognized. In fact, the attorney was told not to sit at the table, and he's not obeying that recommendation," Paul said. "This is the way Anthony Fauci wants to be remembered: for a lawyer not listening to the rules."
"Security, please remove him from the room," the senator added.
Paul threatens Fauci with charges of obstructing Congress
Bart Jansen
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, threatened to pursue criminal charges of obstruction against Fauci despite his pardon for government service and his invoking the Fifth Amendment in refusing to testify.
Before leaving office in 2025, former President Joe Biden pardoned Fauci for actions dating to 2014, but he is vulnerable to charges such as perjury going forward. Paul said he denied Fauci’s assertion of privilege and directed him to answer questions anyway.
When Fauci continued to refuse to testify, Paul said the committee would pursue potential charges against him.
“It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress,” Paul said. “There will be repercussions.”
Paul peppers Fauci with questions despite his refusal to answer
Bart Jansen
Despite Fauci’s refusal to answer questions, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, peppered the former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases with questions about mpox research, the possible CIA transfer of funds to his agency and research into how avian flu jumped to mammals.
Paul focused on whether the benefits of the research into how viruses are spread were worth the risk.
“On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution,” Fauci replied to each question.
Fauci refuses to answer questions under Fifth Amendment
Bart Jansen
Fauci declined to answer questions from the committee based on his constitutional Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.
Republican lawmakers led by Sen. Rand Paul have accused Fauci of lying about research into the COVID-19 pandemic and threatened to charge him with perjury if he lied at the hearing.
Before leaving office in 2025, former President Joe Biden had pardoned Fauci for any of his actions dating to 2014. But Fauci could face charges going forward.
“On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution,” Fauci said.
Interest in the Fauci hearing runs high
Bart Jansen
Interest in the hearing was running high in the Dirksen Senate Office Building, where a line of spectators stretched down the hall for a chance at a seat in Room 342.
Television crews jostled for hallway interviews with arriving lawmakers.
And Capitol police officers were directing traffic, to keep the hallway clear enough to walk.
Trump blasts Fauci for 'CRAZY!' ideas and says he urged Biden to sideline him
Bart Jansen
Trump blasted Fauci on social media for denying speculation that COVID-19 originated in a Chinese lab and for recommendations such as wearing masks to avoid spreading the virus.
“His ideas were CRAZY!” Trump said. “He made too many bad calls, like on MASKS.”
Trump said he inherited the former director of the National Institute for Allergy and Infectious Diseases during his first term but “with each passing day, relied less and less on him.” Trump said he warned his successor, President Joe Biden, that Fauci was “no good” but he got “destructive power” anyway.

Taking aim at the committee in his opening remarks, Fauci claimed Paul was driven by an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution” to put him “behind bars,” stating he was taking the Fifth on the advice of his legal team.

The scientist, who helped lead the nation’s COVID-19 response, was subpoenaed to testify under oath by Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had an antagonistic relationship with Fauci.
In response to angry, sometimes mocking, questions from Republican senators, Fauci declined to answer more than 100 times, injecting new drama into partisan divides that have festered for years about the origins and handling of the pandemic. In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution.”

U.S. & World
Paul, who has long argued that Fauci should be criminally investigated, based on his belief that the scientist was dishonest in previous testimony to Congress, announced that the committee will vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt for declining to answer questions.
He did not say whether he would push for a criminal contempt referral to federal prosecutors or another charge. He also raised questions about whether Fauci’s pardon affects his eligibility for Fifth Amendment protections.
Republicans accuse Fauci of lying while Democrats say he didn't deserve that
In the combative hearing, Paul and other Republicans accused Fauci of lying in earlier testimony about the coronavirus’s origins, something the longtime National Institutes of Health scientist has forcefully denied. Democrats called the hearing a politically motivated attempt at entrapping Fauci and praised the scientist for his work during the pandemic.
With Fauci declining to answer questions throughout, Paul dominated the approximately three-hour hearing, listing a litany of accusations and detailed questions.
“Today will be the capstone to Anthony Fauci's 40 years of abuse of power at NIH,” Paul said. “History will judge, but the facts as we now know them paint a sordid tale of dishonesty, misjudgment and ultimately the hubris, the likes of which the world has never seen.”
In a heated moment during the hearing, Paul ejected Fauci’s attorney, David Schertler, from the room after he tried to speak without being recognized. In a statement, Schertler said the removal was “outrageous and demonstrates the completely biased and baseless nature of this proceeding.” In another statement, he called Paul’s accusations about Fauci “false and disgraceful.”
Democratic senators praised Fauci and said he didn’t deserve the treatment he was getting.
“This hearing is designed to entrap you,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire.
Paul released some of Fauci's diary
Leading up to the hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary covering the pandemic years. Pointing to some notes about early efforts at understanding how the virus emerged, Paul said on social media that what Fauci “wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories.”
Some of the diary entries – including Fauci’s uncertainty in the pandemic’s earliest days as scientists around the world raced to understand the new virus and how best to curb it before vaccines could be created – already were reflected in a 2024 memoir and in interviews at the time.
But they have nonetheless drawn attention from people who blame Fauci for mask mandates, school closures and other policies they believe infringed on their rights as hundreds of thousands of people were dying.
President Donald Trump on Wednesday wrote on social media that he stopped relying on Fauci over the course of the pandemic because he felt the scientist made bad decisions about masks, shutdowns, and other issues. He later told reporters he watched the entire hearing.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist before entering public office, said on social media that his department had found the diary entries on government property and had given them to the committee.
Dozens of disease experts defend Fauci
Scientists also scrambled to Fauci’s defense ahead of the unusual hearing — the second time he has been back before Congress to discuss pandemic origins since leaving the government in 2022. While the COVID-19 pandemic introduced him to millions of Americans, he talked the nation through numerous outbreaks over decades, including HIV, Ebola and the 2001 anthrax attacks, while advising seven presidents.
In a public letter, more than 150 infectious-disease experts and other scientists wrote that “no credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges” and that they are urging elected officials to “stop these witch-hunts.”
Among topics discussed at Wednesday's hearing was whether NIH-funded research in China may have played a role in how the pandemic started.
Many scientists believe the virus most likely emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people, coming to light when it spread at a wildlife market in the Chinese city of Wuhan. There’s no new scientific evidence supporting the theory that the virus might instead have leaked from a laboratory, a theory Paul champions. A GOP-led subcommittee that studied the question in 2024 found no evidence linking Fauci to wrongdoing.
Fauci has long said publicly that he was open to both theories but that there’s more evidence supporting COVID-19’s natural origins.
Republicans also have accused Fauci of lying about whether his agency funded what's known as gain-of-function research — the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impact — at a lab in Wuhan.
The NIH, for years, gave grants to a New York nonprofit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to work with a Chinese lab studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats. But the definition of gain-of-function covers both general research and especially risky experiments that enhance the ability of potential pandemic viruses to spread or cause severe disease in humans. Fauci has previously stressed he was using the risky experiment definition and that “it would be molecularly impossible” for those bat virus experiments to have turned into the pandemic virus.
Trump, a Republican, paused some federally funded gain-of-function research last year, and on Tuesday his administration announced new rules to tighten oversight.

Updated July 29, 2026 at 12:08 PM PDT
Anthony Fauci declined to answer any questions before a Senate committee focused on the coronavirus pandemic Wednesday morning.
"Although it pains me to do so, because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci said in front of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
Fauci, the country's leading infectious disease specialist during the COVID-19 pandemic, was subpoenaed to appear by Kentucky senator and committee chair Rand Paul. He has long sparred with the senator over the origins of the coronavirus that caused the pandemic.
Days before Wednesday's hearing, Paul released over 1,000 pages of Fauci's private diary entries about his daily life between December 2019 and 2022, accusing him of covering up the origins of COVID-19. The entries span the final years of his tenure as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID). He retired in December 2022.
At the hearing, Fauci pointed out that he has responded to similar questions in previous testimony. And Fauci accused the senator of being obsessed with trying to get him behind bars.
Paul posted the documents over the weekend, took them down on Monday evening and reposted them by Tuesday morning with redactions. Paul also released a 465-page "prequel," a collection of Fauci documents including records and email exchanges from 2001 to 2015.
On his website, Paul pointed to Fauci's entry from Feb. 1, 2020, detailing a conference call between Fauci and prominent scientists.
In his notes, Fauci writes "there was not total agreement" about the virus' origins during the call.
Later in his entries, however, Fauci writes he "is almost certain that the virus evolved naturally from a species jump, even though … I keep an open mind about the possibility of a lab leak," and "that just because two alternatives are possible that does not mean that they are equally probable."
Many scientists say this thought process reflects how their consensus changed as the understanding of COVID-19 evolved.
For the latest stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Debate that won't abate
The hearing follows years of debate about the pandemic's origins, and whether the virus that causes COVID-19 emerged accidentally or intentionally from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, a Chinese laboratory which has studied bat coronaviruses.
The lab is located in the city where the first cases of COVID were recorded.
Paul alleges Fauci's notes show he covered up evidence supporting this "lab leak" theory.
In a thread on X over the weekend, Paul wrote that the diary entries show what Fauci "wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories."
A spokesperson for Fauci sent a document fact-checking Paul's claims and a letter written by Fauci's legal team to Paul last month. In that letter, Fauci's lawyers wrote Paul was waging a "years-long public crusade" against Fauci.
"You are single-mindedly fixating on seeing Dr. Fauci prosecuted for imaginary crimes, and you are so invested in that outcome that you have created a personal brand around it," says the letter, which NPR reviewed.
Paul did not respond to NPR's requests for comment in time for publication. It is also unclear how Paul obtained the Fauci diary documents, though a video posted Tuesday on X by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. mentions digging them "out of 11 separate servers."
Consensus for natural origin
The current scientific consensus is that SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, is likely natural in origin. In a report issued in June 2025, the World Health Organization stated: "the weight of available evidence … suggests zoonotic spillover … either directly from bats or through an intermediate host."
That conclusion was based on three years of research by the 27 members of The WHO Scientific Advisory Group for the Origins of Novel Pathogens.
NPR's reporting has supported that theory. In 2024, we covered an analysis by a team of scientists that included prominent names such as Michael Worobey and Angela Rasmussen. NPR noted that their research, published in the peer-reviewed journal Cell, "shows with unprecedented granularity — down to the individual market stall — that coronavirus-susceptible wildlife and the SARS CoV-2 virus were mingling, along with human beings, in a very specific part of the Wuhan market."
The Trump administration has in the past advanced the theory that the pandemic was caused by the virus escaping the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Leaked cables from the State Department raised concerns about safety protocols at the Wuhan lab.
Supporters of the lab leak theory note scientists' analyses relied on incomplete data provided by the Chinese government.
Among U.S. government agencies, some lean toward supporting a natural origin for the virus, while others — including the Department of Energy and the Federal Bureau of Investigation — support a lab origin, although the former has "low confidence" about its conclusion.
NPR reported at the time that "low confidence" meant "the information used in the analysis is scant, questionable, fragmented, or that solid analytical conclusions cannot be inferred from the information," according to the federal government.
One thing is certain: Six years after the start of the pandemic, there is still debate.
The director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, offers this perspective: "As things stand, all hypotheses must remain on the table, including zoonotic spillover and lab leak. We continue to appeal to China and any other country that has information about the origins of COVID-19 to share that information openly, in the interests of protecting the world from future pandemics."
Paul's claims about Fauci's notes
Paul alleges the notes show Fauci's private consideration of the lab leak theory, while he publicly supported the natural origins theory.
On Paul's website, he points to Fauci's entry from Feb. 1, 2020, detailing a conference call between Fauci and prominent scientists.
In his notes, Fauci writes "there was not total agreement" about the virus' origins during the call.
Later in his entries, however, Fauci writes he "is almost certain that the virus evolved naturally from a species jump, even though… I keep an open mind about the possibility of a lab leak," and "that just because two alternatives are possible that does not mean that they are equally probable."
Many scientists say this thought process reflects how their consensus changed as the understanding of COVID-19 evolved.
Felicia Goodrum, a virologist at Dartmouth College who spoke to NPR on Monday from the American Society for Virology meeting in Minneapolis, says the questions in the early days of the pandemic about the lab leak were "normal scientific questioning," when scientists knew very little about how the virus spread.
"I think that's what we acknowledge that Fauci was doing, that there's of course a plethora of unanswered questions," she said of the early days of the pandemic. Now, though, she says those questions are presented as "some sort of signal of guilt that they knew that this was happening."
Gigi Gronvall, a biosecurity expert and immunologist, similarly says these kinds of questions are part of scientific exploration.
"It's not unusual that people would be entertaining a variety of opinions or thinking about a lot of different theories and holes in their theories as they go forward," she says. "That's kind of what science is all about."
Joseph Kim contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Fauci Pleads the Fifth During a Covid Hearing — Here’s How That Went
sources.text:
- Dr. Fauci repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times, saying he feared the hearing was building a criminal case against him.
- The hearing stemmed from a yearslong feud with Sen. Rand Paul over alleged Wuhan research funding and accusations Dr. Fauci misled Congress.
- Paul released over 1,000 pages of Fauci's journals, citing candid Trump critiques and early virus origin notes Republicans used in questioning.
- A presidential pardon did not eliminate all legal risk, so lawyers advised silence; committee may seek contempt citations and investigations continue.
Dr. Anthony Fauci returned to Capitol Hill Wednesday for one of the most closely watched hearings since ending his over five-decade career. But instead of answering senators' questions, the former top infectious disease official repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right, saying he believed the hearing was designed to build a criminal case against him.
So why is this happening now? While the worst of the Covid-19 pandemic may be over, the political battles surrounding it never really ended. Wednesday's hearing was just the latest chapter in Dr. Fauci's long-running clash with GOP Sen. Rand Paul, who has spent years accusing the former health official of misleading Congress about U.S.-funded coronavirus research in Wuhan, China — allegations Dr. Fauci has consistently denied.
The proceedings also underscored how dramatically Dr. Fauci's standing with many Republicans has shifted since he led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the pandemic. As you might recall, President Trump awarded him a Presidential Commendation for his work on Operation Warp Speed in January 2021. But in the years since, he has become a frequent target of congressional investigations into the federal government's pandemic response.
The showdown came just days after Paul publicly released more than 1,000 pages of Dr. Fauci's pandemic-era journals, which Republicans cited throughout the day. Here's a closer look at what Dr. Fauci said, and didn't say, during the questioning.
What happened at Dr. Fauci's hearing?
After accusing committee Chairman Rand Paul of having an "unhinged obsession" with him in prepared remarks, Dr. Fauci announced he would plead the Fifth on the advice of his lawyers. By the end of the hearing, he had done so over 100 times, according to NBC News.
Much of the questioning centered on the same disputes that have defined Paul and Dr. Fauci's ongoing feud, including allegations that the former health official helped conceal the possibility of a lab leak in Wuhan and misled Congress about government-funded coronavirus research there. Republicans also repeatedly pointed to entries from his recently released pandemic-era journals, arguing they raised new questions about the government's Covid-19 response and his decision-making. But again and again, Dr. Fauci declined to answer.
The repeated refrain seemed to frustrate Republicans. GOP Sen. Josh Hawley called Dr. Fauci a "megalomaniac" and "a liar," while Paul warned there would be "repercussions" if he continued refusing to answer questions.
The confrontation soon extended beyond Dr. Fauci's testimony. At one point, Paul ordered Capitol Police to remove one of his attorneys, David Schertler, after the lawyer repeatedly attempted to speak on his client's behalf without being recognized by the committee.
"Another word, and you're gone," Paul warned before directing officers to escort Schertler out.
The dramatic exchange prompted Democratic members to walk out in protest, accusing Republicans of turning the proceedings into a political spectacle rather than a legitimate oversight hearing.
What was in Dr. Fauci's pandemic-era journals?
The journals themselves became a major focus of Wednesday's proceedings. Last year, Paul subpoenaed 14 federal agencies, including the National Institutes of Health, as part of his investigation. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Monday that his department spent months locating the records across 11 government servers before turning them over to the committee.
The collection includes more than 1,000 pages of near-daily entries from the pandemic's most critical months, offering a behind-the-scenes look at Fauci's decision-making as he helped guide the nation's Covid-19 response under both the Trump and Biden administrations. Kennedy told Fox News the journals reveal a "striking contrast" between Fauci's public statements and his private reflections, a characterization Fauci has not publicly addressed.
The documents offered a window into what Fauci was thinking as the pandemic unfolded. He described President Trump at various points as "rambling," "out of control," and a "total embarrassment." He also reflected on the intense attention he received during the pandemic, writing that his national and international fame had become "explosive."
In one January 2020 note, Fauci suggested Wuhan's seafood market may have acted as an "amplifier" of the outbreak rather than its original source. At the same time, he wrote that he believed the virus most likely spread naturally from animals to humans.
Why did Dr. Fauci plead the Fifth?
Dr. Fauci argued that answering lawmakers' questions could expose him to future legal jeopardy.
His legal team said Sen. Paul had become fixated on Dr. Fauci after the pair's high-profile clashes during the pandemic, including a heated 2021 exchange in which the two accused each other of lying. Schertler argued the hearing was intended not to conduct oversight but to punish the 85-year-old and see him imprisoned.
"The accusations that Chairman Paul continues to propagate are false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable," Schertler said in a statement shared with news outlets.
Some readers may wonder why Dr. Fauci invoked the Fifth after receiving a preemptive presidential pardon. In the final hours of his presidency, President Biden granted Dr. Fauci a pardon covering potential federal offenses committed before Jan. 20, 2025, saying he wanted to protect him from what he viewed as politically motivated prosecution.
But the pardon had limits. It did not prevent Congress from investigating Dr. Fauci, subpoenaing him, or requiring him to testify under oath. And according to his lawyers, it did not eliminate all potential legal risks associated with answering lawmakers' questions, which is why they advised him to repeatedly invoke his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.
Legal experts say that approach was not unusual. The Fifth Amendment protects people from being compelled to provide testimony that could incriminate them in a criminal case. Attorneys often advise witnesses to invoke the privilege broadly rather than answer some questions but not others because selective testimony can create additional legal risk. As criminal defense lawyer Steven Clark told USA Today, witnesses generally can't "pick and choose" which questions to answer.
Invoking the Fifth, however, is not an admission of guilt. The U.S. Supreme Court has repeatedly held that a person cannot be found guilty simply because they exercised their Fifth Amendment rights. As the Court wrote in Ohio v. Reiner, "one of the Fifth Amendment's basic functions is to protect innocent persons who otherwise might be ensnared by ambiguous circumstances."
What happens next?
The hearing may have ended without answers, but the investigation is far from over. Afterwards, Paul told reporters he plans to hold a committee vote next week to recommend holding Dr. Fauci in contempt of Congress for refusing to testify.
Whether the effort ultimately succeeds — or whether prosecutors pursue any further action—remains to be seen. It's also unclear whether Dr. Fauci will be called back before the committee. But Wednesday's proceedings underscored one thing: More than three years after the Covid public health emergency ended, congressional scrutiny of the government's pandemic response — and Dr. Fauci's role in it — shows little sign of fading.

Fauci invokes the Fifth Amendment and declines to testify in GOP-led Senate panel’s COVID-19 hearing
WASHINGTON (AP) — Dr. Anthony Fauci on Wednesday invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer questions from senators in a Republican-led committee hearing about his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The move injects new drama into the lingering tensions between Fauci and Republican lawmakers over his handling of the coronavirus pandemic and accusations he lied about the origins of COVID-19, which he denies.
Fauci was set to answer lawmakers’ questions after being subpoenaed by Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had a fraught relationship with the now-retired infectious-disease expert and led the charge seeking that he testify, again, under oath.
Fauci’s decision to invoke the Fifth, at least for now, sidesteps calls for his prosecution if he is accused of lying at Wednesday’s hearing, part of a yearslong campaign for his arrest spearheaded by some Republicans in Congress. Though he received a presidential pardon from Democrat Joe Biden, some of Fauci’s critics have suggested he could still face charges if he perjures himself under oath.
His refusal to answer questions may also further inflame partisan divides that have festered for years about the origins and handling of the pandemic, which was declared by the World Health Organization in March 2020.
Fauci, who helped lead the nation’s COVID-19 response, has long been a target of those frustrations. But to his supporters he is an emblem of sound scientific expertise.
In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution.”
“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this Committee is to prompt me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said, adding that while it pains him to do so, he is following his attorney’s advice by taking the Fifth.
Paul releases some of Fauci’s diary
Paul in his opening statement sought to build the case that Fauci helped produce the COVID-19 pandemic by approving funding of research on virus mutations and then covered up his complicity.
Democratic Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the committee’s ranking member, said the hearing was a partisan exercise that looked backward instead of focusing on current national security challenges.
Leading up to the hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s personal diary covering the pandemic years. Pointing to some notes about early efforts at understanding how the virus emerged, Paul wrote on the social media platform X that what Fauci “wrote privately and what he told the country are two different stories.”
Some of the diary entries – including Fauci’s uncertainty in the pandemic’s earliest days as scientists around the world raced to understand the new virus and how best to curb it before vaccines could be created – already were reflected in a 2024 memoir and in interviews at the time.
But they have nonetheless drawn attention from people who blame Fauci for mask mandates, school closures and other policies they believe infringed on their rights as hundreds of thousands of people were dying.
Ahead of the hearing, President Donald Trump wrote on social media that he stopped relying on Fauci over the course of the pandemic because he felt Fauci made bad decisions on masks, shutdowns and other issues.
In a statement, Fauci’s attorney David Schertler said Paul’s accusations are “false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable.”
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist before he entered public office, said Monday that his department gave the diary entries, which were created on a government computer, to the committee. He told a Fox News Channel host that he thought Fauci might lie before the committee, opening him to perjury prosecution.
Paul told Fauci that he may still face repercussions for obstructing a congressional investigation by refusing to testify. That could include a contempt of Congress citation, which would be referred to the Justice Department for consideration.
Scientists scrambled to Fauci’s defense ahead of the unusual hearing — the second time the longtime National Institutes of Health scientist has been back before Congress to discuss pandemic origins since leaving the government in 2022. While the COVID-19 pandemic introduced him to millions of Americans, he talked the nation through numerous outbreaks over decades, including HIV, Ebola and the 2001 anthrax attacks, while advising seven presidents.
Some disease experts criticize the accusations against Fauci
In a public letter, more than 150 infectious-disease experts and other scientists wrote that “no credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges” and that they are “urging our elected representatives in Congress stop these witch-hunts.”
The expected crux of Wednesday’s hearing was whether NIH-funded research in China may have played a role in how the pandemic started.
Many scientists believe the virus most likely emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people, coming to light when it spread at a wildlife market in the Chinese city of Wuhan. There’s no new scientific information supporting that the virus might instead have leaked from a laboratory, a theory Paul champions. A GOP-led subcommittee that studied the question in 2024 did not find any evidence linking Fauci to wrongdoing.
Fauci has long said publicly that he was open to both theories but that there’s more evidence supporting COVID-19’s natural origins, the way other deadly viruses including coronavirus cousins SARS and MERS jumped into people.
Republicans also have accused Fauci of lying about whether his agency funded what’s known as gain of function research — the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impact — at a lab in Wuhan.
The NIH for years gave grants to a New York nonprofit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to work with a Chinese lab studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats. But the definition of gain of function covers both general research and especially risky experiments to enhance the ability of potential pandemic viruses to spread or cause severe disease in humans. Fauci has previously stressed he was using the risky experiment definition and that “it would be molecularly impossible” for those bat virus experiments to have turned into the pandemic virus.
Trump, a Republican, last year paused some federally funded gain of function research, and on Tuesday his administration announced new rules to tighten oversight.

It was the latest twist in the long-running feud between Anthony Fauci, who spent decades as the nation's top expert in infectious disease, and Republican Senator Rand Paul, who insists on unsubstantiated claims that the origins of the pandemic began in a lab and were covered up.
Paul had subpoenaed the now-retired Fauci to testify before the committee, and prior to the hearing released thousands of pages of the immunologist's personal diary.
Citing Paul's "obsession" with him, Fauci said he would invoke the Fifth Amendment, refraining from answering questions to avoid self-incrimination, adding that it "pains me to do so."
Fauci indicated his lawyers believed Paul intended to entrap him in a slip-up that could result in perjury charges.
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote 'behind bars,'" Fauci said.
Fauci, 85, noted in his opening statement that he had testified before Congress more than 200 times over nearly four decades, saying "I proved that I believe in and respect the value of legitimate congressional oversight."
Paul opened with a tirade against Fauci, repeating accusations that under Fauci's watch at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, the US funded so-called "gain-of-function" research in China that triggered the spread of Covid-19.
The senator insists Fauci lied about that to Congress, which he has repeatedly denied.
More than six years after the pandemic's onset, the debate over whether Covid-19 leaked from a lab remains intense. Fauci has maintained that the virus had natural origins, even if he's said he is open to the idea of a lab leak.
Some panel lawmakers criticized the proceedings, including Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan, who said the hearing was designed to "entrap" Fauci.
Paul warned Fauci of "repercussions" for his use of the Fifth Amendment. When Fauci's lawyer attempted to speak on his client's behalf, Paul ordered him removed.
As the approximately three-hour long hearing closed Paul said the committee would vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress for invoking the Fifth, a process that could open increasingly complicated legal puzzles, not least given former President Joe Biden's preemptive pardon of the government scientist.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal meanwhile called the proceedings the result of a "vendetta" and that use of the Fifth must be "respected."
Law professor Tracey Maclin of the University of Florida dubbed "nonsensical" any notion that staying silent was a bad look.
"If his lawyers told him to take the Fifth, that's what he should do," Maclin told AFP, emphasizing that invoking the right was not at all an indication of guilt.
Ahead of the doctor's appearance, a group of more than 150 scientists, physicians and public health activists signed an open letter calling on lawmakers to "stop the on-going vilification and harassment" of scientists, while denouncing "absurd" accusations against Fauci.
US President Donald Trump weighed in on Truth Social, saying Fauci's "ideas were CRAZY!" in the pandemic's early days and accusing him of "trying to protect China."
Fauci's diary excerpts don't offer clear evidence regarding Covid's origins. Rather, the text depicts Fauci grappling with the escalating public health crisis as scientific hypotheses were rapidly evolving.
The journal also offers a glimpse into his deteriorating relationship with Trump, whom he advised during the president's first term.
"Trump getting out of control in pushing to open up the country and get the economy back before election day," Fauci wrote in a passage dated May 2020. "He is desperate. This is all about reelection."
The diary traces Fauci's overnight fame, which thrust him into the spotlight as a lifelong bureaucrat-turned-star who enjoyed attention from celebrities.
But he also details pressures that his day job and his notoriety carried.
"The vicious assault on me continues," Fauci wrote on June 6, 2021. "The entire extreme right wing Republican group in the House and Senate have completely sold their soul to the infinitely lying ex-president trump."
